posts.title: An attitude indicator failing slowly
posts.headline: Your attitude indicator can be wrong without looking broken.
posts.alt: An attitude indicator failing slowly: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Your attitude indicator can be wrong without looking broken. The picture shows the vacuum system as Figure 8-20 draws it: heading indicator, attitude indicator, suction gauge, air filter, relief valve, pump and the hoses connecting them, the two gyro instruments side by side between the filter and the pump; the vacuum pump cold and still, nothing flowing in any hose; the suction gauge needle resting well below the short green arc that marks its normal range; the attitude indicator intact and convincing but showing a left bank as the FAA draws one: horizon and bank scale turned together, the orange miniature airplane level. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Would you spot an attitude indicator drifting slowly after a vacuum failure?

After a vacuum pump failure the gyros slow down, and the attitude indicator can wander and show a wrong picture while still looking normal. Cross-check it against every other instrument. An electric turn coordinator still shows direction and rate of turn. Many small aircraft have no vacuum warning, so watch the suction gauge for a reading below its normal range.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: After a vacuum pump failure the attitude and heading indicators can fail progressively: as their gyros slow down they may wander, so the attitude indicator can show a wrong picture without looking broken and lead an unsuspecting pilot into an unusual attitude.

Where the vacuum system drives the attitude and heading indicators and the electrical system drives the turn coordinator, the turn coordinator keeps showing the direction and rate of turn while the attitude indicator wanders. It does not display a specific angle of bank.

Many small aircraft have no warning system for a vacuum failure, so the pilot has to watch the suction gauge: a reading below its normal range means the vacuum system is not supplying the suction the gyros need.
posts.intent: When the vacuum pump quits, the attitude indicator does not go blank; its gyro spins down and the picture drifts away from the truth while still looking like a picture.

article.heading: Why a failing attitude indicator looks normal
paragraphs: Imagine you're in cloud, with no outside horizon to look at. Your best picture of pitch, whether the nose is up or down, and bank, how far the wings tilt, comes from one instrument.
That instrument is the attitude indicator. Its face shows a miniature aircraft set against a horizon bar. The handbook calls it reliable and the most realistic flight instrument on the panel.

That trust is what makes a failed vacuum pump, the engine-driven pump that supplies this instrument's suction, so dangerous. When it quits, the instrument can show a wrong picture without looking broken.

An unsuspecting pilot who follows that picture can be led into a dangerous unusual attitude, a pitch or bank far from what was intended. Getting out of it then takes a partial panel recovery, flown on whatever instruments are still working.

article.heading: How the gyro holds the horizon
paragraphs: Inside the attitude indicator is a gyro, a wheel kept spinning in a horizontal plane. The horizon bar on the face is fixed to that gyro.
A spinning gyro resists anything that would tip its path of spin. This resistance to being tipped is called rigidity in space, and the instrument depends on it.

So when you pitch or bank, the gyro and its horizon bar stay level with the true horizon. The airplane actually rotates around the spinning gyro, not the other way around. Read the miniature aircraft against the bar, and you are reading your airplane against the real horizon.
All of this assumes the gyro is spinning fast enough. In a vacuum-driven attitude indicator, the suction that keeps it at speed comes from the vacuum system.

article.heading: What happens as the gyro slows
paragraphs: That suction comes from the vacuum pump, which is driven mechanically off the engine. Occasionally a pump fails, and with it go the attitude indicator and the heading indicator, the gyro instrument showing which way you're pointed.
The gyros don't stop dead. Once the vacuum system stops making enough suction to hold their speed, they begin to slow down.

As a gyro slows, it is pushed off its plane of spin more easily. It can precess, which means it creeps away from the position it was holding. It is simply no longer spinning fast enough to keep its alignment.

That is why the handbook says these instruments can fail progressively. As the gyros slow, the attitude picture and the heading may wander, and an autopilot connected to them can move the airplane wrongly.

In the handbook's figure of a vacuum failure, the airplane is level at 2,000 feet above mean sea level. A pilot who misses the off or failed flags, the warnings on the instrument faces, may still read a left turn. Rolling out of a turn that isn't happening puts a level airplane into a bank.

figure.caption: The vacuum pump pulls air through the filter and the two gyro instruments, and the suction gauge shows how much suction it is making. The electric turn coordinator is not on that line, so a failed pump leaves it working.
figure.alt: The vacuum pump pulls air through the filter and the two gyro instruments, and the suction gauge shows how much suction it is making. The electric turn coordinator is not on that line, so a failed pump leaves it working.

article.heading: How the suction gauge warns you
paragraphs: Many small aircraft have no warning system for a vacuum failure. Some aircraft do have a warning light for low vacuum, but others have only a gauge that shows the suction.

In those airplanes the suction gauge is the warning, so it belongs in your cross-check, the habit of moving your eyes across the instruments. A reading below its normal range means low suction, and the gyros aren't getting what they need.
The gauge reads the cause directly. The attitude indicator shows only the effect, and it may show it without looking broken.

article.heading: Why the turn coordinator keeps working
paragraphs: The turn coordinator shows how fast you're turning and which way. Picture a panel where the vacuum system drives the attitude and heading indicators and the electrical system drives the turn coordinator. The handbook's own drawing of a turn coordinator has D.C. ELEC. printed on its face.
In that panel, a vacuum pump failure leaves the turn coordinator alone. It keeps showing the direction and rate of turn even while the attitude indicator wanders.
Rate of turn is how many degrees your heading changes each second. Marks on the instrument's left and right sides show a standard-rate turn, defined as 3° per second.
Know what it leaves out. It doesn't show the angle of bank, and its face carries the words NO PITCH INFORMATION.

Once you know the attitude indicator has failed, the turn coordinator becomes your reference for turning. When the small airplane on its face sits level, it shows no rate of turn, so your heading is holding steady.

article.heading: Catching the failure in your cross-check
paragraphs: Without a warning light, a failure usually gives itself away as a disagreement. The attitude indicator stops agreeing with the instruments that back it up.

One quick check compares the attitude indicator with the turn coordinator and the vertical speed indicator, which shows climb or descent. That single comparison sets three separate systems against each other, the suction system, the electrical system and the static system. The static system is the one that feeds the vertical speed indicator, along with the airspeed indicator and altimeter.

The fault can be a single instrument or a whole system. A vacuum failure is a system failure, so expect both the attitude and heading indicators to be affected. A suction gauge below its normal range confirms which system it is.

article.heading: Flying on once the gyros have failed
paragraphs: Keep control of the airplane while you work out what has failed. Speed up your cross-check and include every flight instrument in it.
Then fly on the instruments that still work. Covering the failed attitude and heading indicators may help, because a wrong picture you can't see can't lead you anywhere.
Look for a fix next. Check the power source, switch to a backup or alternate system if there is one, and reset the instrument if you can.
Then tell air traffic control what has happened. If you need to, declare an emergency early, while the situation is still within your ability to recover.
The handbook calls it important to practice instrument flight without the attitude and heading indicators. Do that, and partial panel flying won't be new to you when a pump quits for real.

posts.title: An upsloping runway and a low approach
posts.headline: An upsloping runway fools you into flying low.
posts.alt: An upsloping runway and a low approach: an illustrated diagram for pilots. An upsloping runway fools you into flying low. The picture shows a runway that visibly slopes uphill away from the approaching aircraft; the solid aircraft on a shallow path clearly below the normal approach; a translucent ghost aircraft on the normal approach path above the solid one, as the comparison; two thin approach path lines converging on the runway threshold, one visibly lower than the other. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Why does an upsloping runway leave you lower than normal on final?

A runway that climbs away from you makes a normal approach look high. Believe that picture and you'll ease down to lose height you never had, until the whole approach sits below the normal path. The error feels like a correction.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: An upsloping runway creates the illusion of being higher on the approach than actual.
Flying that illusion produces a lower than normal approach.
posts.intent: An upsloping runway makes the approach look steeper than it is, so the correction is to fly lower.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 17

figure_key.label: NORMAL PATH, FEELS HIGH
figure_key.points_at: The ghost aircraft on the upper, normal approach path.

figure_key.label: LOWER THAN NORMAL
figure_key.points_at: The solid aircraft on the lower, shallower approach path.

figure_key.label: RUNWAY RISES AWAY

article.heading: What an upsloping runway makes you feel
paragraphs: Picture a runway whose far end sits higher than the end you touch down on. The ground under your approach may rise toward it as well.

An upsloping runway, upsloping terrain, or both can give you the illusion of being higher than you really are. The FAA's pilot handbook, FAA-H-8083-25, files this among the optical illusions it ties mainly to landing.
The pilot handbook calls it the runway and terrain slopes illusion. It gives no figure for how much slope it takes to fool you, only which way the error runs.
Downsloping runways and downsloping approach terrain can have the opposite effect. They can make you feel lower than you are, which leads to a higher approach.

table.caption: Which way each slope tilts your judgment, from Figure 17-7 of FAA-H-8083-25 and the text beside it.

article.heading: How you judge your approach by eye
paragraphs: FAA-H-8083-3, the FAA's airplane flying handbook, teaches you to judge your descent partly from the runway ahead. Seen from the air, its rectangle looks like a trapezoid, with the far end narrower and the edges converging. That effect is called perspective.
On a stabilized approach, one held at a constant angle toward a chosen point on the runway, the trapezoid keeps its shape. It only grows as you close in.
On a shallow approach the runway seems to shorten and widen. On a steep one it seems to stretch longer and narrower.
You also watch the aiming point, the spot on the ground your descent line points at. On a constant-angle path it seems to stay still, and its distance below the horizon doesn't change.
Every one of these cues comes through your eyes. The pilot handbook warns that the surface below and the air around you on landing can create illusions of being on the wrong approach path.

figure.caption: The outline keeps its shape while the angle holds and changes as soon as the angle does.
figure.alt: The outline keeps its shape while the angle holds and changes as soon as the angle does.

article.heading: Why feeling high leaves you low
paragraphs: Neither handbook says which of those cues an upslope distorts. The pilot handbook says what you end up believing, which is that you're higher than you are.

When you feel high on final, the natural move is to come down. Over an upsloping runway that move fixes a problem you don't have. A pilot who doesn't recognize the illusion will fly a lower approach than normal.
The slope paragraph stops there, but the runway width illusion ends the same way. A runway narrower than usual can also make you feel high and lead you into a lower approach.
For that case the pilot handbook names the risks of flying low. They are striking objects along the approach path and landing short.
The same chapter says illusions are among the most often cited contributors to fatal aviation accidents. It says so of visual illusions as a group, without singling out slope.

article.heading: Learning the slope before you arrive
paragraphs: The first defense the pilot handbook lists is to expect visual illusions on approaches to unfamiliar airports. It singles out approaches at night or in adverse weather.

Before you go, read the airport diagram and the Chart Supplement U.S., the publication formerly called the Airport/Facility Directory. The pilot handbook sends you to both for runway slope, terrain and lighting.
Check the ground on the approach path as well as the runway itself. Upsloping terrain can create the same illusion, alone or together with an upsloping runway.
If you can, fly over an unfamiliar airport and look at it before you land. The pilot handbook calls this an aerial visual inspection.

article.heading: Cross-checking the view on final
paragraphs: On final, don't fly the picture alone. Refer to the altimeter often on every approach, by day and by night.

Use a Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI) or a Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI) whenever one is available. The pilot handbook lists both as a visual reference, alongside an electronic glideslope, the vertical guidance on some instrument approaches.
It also points to the visual descent point (VDP), a point marked on many nonprecision instrument approach charts. Those are approaches flown without an electronic glideslope.
At the end of an instrument approach you switch from instruments to outside cues for the landing. That switch is why the pilot handbook wants you alert to these illusions.
Watch for distraction as well. The pilot handbook warns that an emergency or anything else pulling you from usual procedures raises your chance of an approach accident.

article.heading: Fixing a low approach once you spot it
paragraphs: The aiming point tells you when you've gone low. If it seems to creep up toward the horizon, the true aiming point is closer than it looks. You're undershooting, heading short of where you aimed.
The flying handbook's fix is power and pitch together. Add power and raise the nose to level off, holding the correct airspeed. That can take a large increase in power.
As you meet the glide path, the line you meant to descend along, reduce power and lower the nose to stay on it. Catch the error early and the corrections left for short final stay small.

Two shortcuts make it worse. Raising the nose without adding power bleeds off airspeed, and ends in an excessive rate of descent, a low-altitude stall, or both. Retracting the flaps can cause a sudden loss of lift and an excessive sink rate.
If you're very low, a stabilized approach may no longer be possible. The normal answer then is a go-around, abandoning the landing and climbing away to set up again.

figure.caption: Whether you level off and rejoin the path or go around depends on how low you are.
figure.alt: Whether you level off and rejoin the path or go around depends on how low you are.

posts.title: Centre of gravity aft of the limit
posts.headline: Past the aft limit, you have less nose-down elevator.
posts.alt: Centre of gravity aft of the limit: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Past the aft limit, you have less nose-down elevator. The picture shows a light high-wing single seen side-on, nose still above a level horizon; its elevator deflected fully trailing-edge down; streamlines breaking into curling eddies above the solid aeroplane's wing; a small red CG marker sitting behind a pale aft-limit tick on the fuselage. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: What happens to stall recovery when the CG is aft of the limit?

Load the airplane behind its rearward CG limit and longitudinal stability drops. Stall recovery gets harder too. The elevator has less authority to lower the nose, and lowering the nose is how the recovery begins.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Loading aft of the rearward CG limit reduces longitudinal stability.
Stall recovery is degraded with an aft CG because elevator authority to lower the nose is reduced.
posts.intent: An aft CG shortens the tail's lever arm, so the aeroplane becomes less stable in pitch and harder to recover from a stall.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 10

article.heading: What the centre of gravity is
paragraphs: Picture your loaded aeroplane hanging from a single hook. The centre of gravity, or CG, is the one point where you could hang it and it would balance.

The CG doesn't have to stay in one place. Where it sits depends on how the weight is spread through the aeroplane, so it shifts when load is moved or used up. A heavy bag moved aft takes the CG aft with it.

Balance side to side counts too, but the FAA's handbook treats the fore-and-aft position as the one that matters most. With the CG too far forward, the aeroplane is nose heavy. Too far aft, it's tail heavy.
The manufacturer sets a forward limit and an aft limit for the CG. The distance between them is the CG range, and the CG must sit inside it during flight.

article.heading: What the aft limit is set for
paragraphs: The aft limit is the furthest back the CG can sit and still suit the most demanding manoeuvre or operation. In other words, it's drawn for the worst case.
You'll find the limits in the aeroplane's Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) or its aircraft specification. They're also in the aircraft flight manual (AFM) or pilot's operating handbook (POH).

A regulation, 14 CFR 23.23, requires that safe ranges of weight and CG be established for the aeroplane. The manufacturer supplies them, and they go into the approved AFM, TCDS or aircraft specifications.

The aft limit isn't always one fixed spot. For some aeroplanes both limits may move as the aeroplane's total weight changes. They may also change for aerobatic flight, for retracting the landing gear, or for special loads and devices that alter how it flies.

article.heading: Why a tail-heavy aeroplane is less stable
paragraphs: Fly into turbulence and a bump knocks the nose up. A stable aeroplane then rights itself, with the nose settling back where it was. That ability to right itself in pitch, nose up and nose down, is longitudinal stability.
As the CG moves aft, that ability shrinks. The aeroplane becomes less stable, and less able to right itself after turbulence or after you manoeuvre.
The handbook calls the effect of tail-heavy loading on longitudinal stability serious. The less the aeroplane corrects by itself, the more correcting is left to you.

At the far end, the handbook says it's possible the pilot could not control an aeroplane whose CG made it unstable. Extreme control difficulty is also on its list of possible effects of a CG aft of the range.

article.heading: How stalls and spins change
paragraphs: Now suppose the tail-heavy aeroplane stalls, or enters a spin. Tail-heavy loading reduces your capability to recover from either one.
Put simply, a recovery that works with the CG within limits works less well once the CG is behind the aft limit. The handbook states this outright for tail-heavy loading.
The stall itself may be worse too. Among the possible effects of a CG aft of the allowable range, the handbook lists violent stall characteristics.
Both of these come from the same tail-heavy load as the loss of stability. On one flight, the aeroplane is less able to right itself and you're less able to recover it from a stall or spin.

article.heading: Why very light controls are a hazard
paragraphs: In a tail-heavy aeroplane it takes very little push or pull on the controls to move them. That push or pull is the control force, and tail-heavy loading makes it very light.

Light controls sound pleasant, but the handbook counts them as another undesirable trait. With so little force needed, it's easy to overstress the aeroplane, loading its structure beyond what it's built for, without meaning to.

When the aeroplane is out of balance fore and aft, the natural fix is a trim change that takes away the pressure you're holding. Too much trim costs you something, though. It makes the aeroplane less efficient in the air, and it shortens the travel the control has left in the direction you trimmed.
Flying an aeroplane that's out of balance can also leave you more tired. That fatigue has its own cost to the safety and efficiency of the flight.

article.heading: How the load moves the CG
paragraphs: Most of the time, you're the one who decides where the CG ends up. Where the baggage and cargo go sets it, and so does who sits in which seat.
If the loading comes out tail heavy, the handbook's fix is the obvious one. Put the heavy passengers in the forward seats.
How far fuel burn moves the CG depends on where the tanks are. In most small aeroplanes the fuel is in the wings, very near the CG, so the loaded CG hardly moves as it burns.
Changes to the aeroplane itself move the CG too. Adding or removing equipment shifts it, and without up-to-date weight and balance records you have nothing to base the calculation on.

article.heading: Checking the CG before you fly
paragraphs: In many modern aeroplanes you can't fill every seat, baggage compartment and tank and stay inside the weight and balance limits. With the maximum passenger load aboard, you'll often have to carry less fuel or less baggage.
Before any flight, work out the weight and balance with the manufacturer's procedure and the charts in the AFM. If the loaded CG isn't within limits, move items before you attempt the flight.

The Part 91 operating rules have no specific requirement for a weight and balance calculation before every flight. What 14 CFR 91.9 does require is that you, as pilot in command, comply with the AFM's operating limits. Those include weight and balance.

posts.title: The room VFR leaves around a cloud
posts.headline: In Class D, give a cloud 2,000 feet sideways.
posts.alt: The room VFR leaves around a cloud: an illustrated diagram for pilots. In Class D, give a cloud 2,000 feet sideways. The picture shows a single cumulus with a sunlit top and a level, shadowed base; a thin dashed boundary around the cloud, farthest out at the sides, less far above the top, closest under the base; a horizontal dimension line that is visibly the longest, about twice the line above the cloud and four times the line below it; two vertical dimension lines, one above the cloud top and a shorter one under the base. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Here's how much room VFR keeps from a cloud, class by class.

Class D wants more room above a cloud than below it, and the most room of all sideways. Class C matches it, as does Class E below 10,000 feet MSL. Class B asks only for clear of clouds, and that habit is easy to carry into Class D, where the numbers apply.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: VFR cloud clearance requirements differ by airspace class and altitude.
In Class C, Class D and Class E below 10,000 feet MSL the requirement is 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally.
Class B is different: the requirement there is to remain clear of clouds, with no numeric separation.
posts.intent: The required clearance is a set of distances that differ by airspace class, and in the classes that have them the horizontal figure is the largest.

figure_key.label: 1,000 FEET ABOVE
figure_key.points_at: The vertical dimension line rising from the cloud's sunlit top to the dashed boundary above it.

figure_key.label: 500 FEET BELOW

article.heading: What cloud clearance asks you to keep
paragraphs: Picture yourself flying VFR, under visual flight rules, in Class D airspace. A single cloud sits ahead of you and a little to the left.
The sky is split into lettered airspace classes, and the weather rules are written class by class. In Class D, the rule for that cloud is a set of three distances.
You stay at least 500 feet below the cloud, 1,000 feet above it and 2,000 feet away from it horizontally. Break any one of the three and you are closer than the rule allows.
Think of it as a buffer the cloud carries around with it. It's thin underneath, thicker on top and widest out to the sides.

The figures come from 14 CFR 91.155, the basic VFR weather minimums. Its table pairs each airspace class and altitude band with two things. One is a flight visibility, how far you must be able to see, and the other is a distance from clouds.

article.heading: Classes C, D and E share one set
paragraphs: The 500, 1,000 and 2,000 set belongs to more than Class D. Class C uses the same three figures. So does Class E, as long as you're below 10,000 feet MSL, meaning measured from mean sea level.
All three also ask for 3 statute miles of flight visibility. One set of numbers carries you from Class C through Class D and out into low Class E.
In each of them the horizontal figure is the largest. At 2,000 feet, it's more than the distances above and below added together.

Level flight shows why that matters. Hold your altitude and fly toward a cloud, and only the horizontal gap is shrinking. The vertical figures only come into play when you climb, descend, or pass over or under it.
So the 2,000 feet is the number you spend first in cruise. That's why the short version for Class D is to give a cloud 2,000 feet sideways.

figure.alt: In Class C, D and E below 10,000 feet MSL, the room beside a cloud is four times the room below it.

article.heading: How Class E changes above 10,000 feet
paragraphs: Climb to 10,000 feet MSL or higher in Class E and the buffer grows on every side except the top. It becomes 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 1 statute mile horizontal.
The visibility you need goes up as well, from 3 statute miles to 5 statute miles. Up there you must see farther and keep farther away, both at once.
The sideways figure is still the biggest, since a statute mile is well beyond 1,000 feet. That holds in every row of the table that gives distances at all.
At the bottom edge of Class E, one short rule settles which row you use. Fly right at its floor, called the base altitude, and you count as being in the airspace directly underneath.

article.heading: What clear of clouds means in Class B
paragraphs: Now put the same cloud inside Class B, the airspace that generally surrounds the nation's busiest airports. The requirement here is to remain clear of clouds, with no number attached.
There's no 500 feet below, no 1,000 feet above and no 2,000 feet sideways. You keep out of the cloud itself, and you still need 3 statute miles of flight visibility.
Class B isn't the only place the table uses those words. Class G uses them too, low down and by day, and the last section comes back to that.
Class A is the one class with no cloud figure of any kind. Both of its columns simply read not applicable.

Class B also has an entry rule the weather table doesn't show. You need an ATC clearance, meaning permission from air traffic control, before you go in. Once inside, VFR pilots get sequencing and separation, meaning controllers order them and keep them apart from other aircraft.

article.heading: When a Class B clearance points at cloud
paragraphs: Inside Class B, a controller may assign you a route, a heading or an altitude. Picture one of those pointing straight at a cloud.

Being separated from traffic doesn't change the cloud rule. The AIM, the Aeronautical Information Manual, says the separation service leaves the 91.155 weather minimums as your responsibility. In Class B, that minimum is clear of clouds.
So spotting the problem is your job. If an assigned route, heading or altitude would put you in cloud, tell approach control. Get a revised clearance or instruction and fly that instead.
The separation itself depends on radar. If the radar goes out, the service is suspended and you are told, but clear of clouds still applies.

article.heading: Class G changes with height and daylight
paragraphs: Class G is the one class where the cloud rule depends on your height above the ground and on whether it's day or night. The table splits it at 1,200 feet above the surface, whatever your MSL altitude.

Down low, at 1,200 feet or less above the surface, an airplane by day needs 1 statute mile of visibility. It only has to stay clear of clouds. At night the full set comes back, 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontal, with 3 statute miles.

One night exception sits right beside the runway, still below 1,200 feet over the surface. In an airport traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway, an airplane may fly clear of clouds. That holds when visibility is under 3 statute miles but not below 1 statute mile.
Above 1,200 feet over the surface and below 10,000 feet MSL, the 500, 1,000 and 2,000 set applies day and night. Only the visibility changes, 1 statute mile by day and 3 statute miles at night.
Once you're also at 10,000 feet MSL or higher, Class G matches high Class E. You need 5 statute miles, 1,000 feet below and above, and 1 statute mile sideways.

posts.headline: Clear of the cloud isn't clear of its wind.
posts.alt: The gust front ahead of a thunderstorm: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Clear of the cloud isn't clear of its wind. The picture shows a thunderstorm on the left with a dark rain shaft and a clean right-hand cloud edge; pale streamlines dropping out of the rain and running along the ground well past the cloud edge; a curling dust roll marking the gust front's leading edge far to the right of the cloud; open sky with no cloud above the solid aircraft, which sits inside the streamlines. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: What's a gust front, and how far ahead of the storm can it run?

A thunderstorm's downdraft hits the ground and spreads outward as a gust front. That wind can run many miles ahead of the cell. It is easy to read clear air around the cloud as distance from the storm, but the outflow may already be under you.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: A thunderstorm's downdraft spreads outward at the surface as a gust front that can precede the cell by many miles.
Staying clear of the visible cloud is not the same as staying clear of the storm's wind.
posts.intent: The hazard reaches well ahead of the visible cloud, because the outflow spreads out along the surface before the cell arrives.

figure_key.label: GUST FRONT, MILES AHEAD

article.heading: Why missing the cloud isn't enough
paragraphs: Picture a thunderstorm off your left wing, with open blue sky between you and the edge of its cloud. You've given the cloud plenty of room. Then the airplane starts to buck in gusts you didn't plan for.

Those gusts belong to the storm's outflow, the cool air it has driven down to the ground and out along the surface. The outflow spreads well ahead of the storm, into sky that can look perfectly clear.
The cloud is only the part of a thunderstorm you can see. Its wind reaches past that edge, so staying clear of the cloud isn't the same as staying clear of its wind.

article.heading: How a storm makes its own wind
paragraphs: Every thunderstorm comes from a cumulonimbus, the towering cloud that makes lightning and thunder. A storm is made of one or more cells, each a column of rising and sinking air with its own life cycle.
A cell starts with an updraft, a current of warm air rising through the cloud. In this first stage, called towering cumulus, the updraft can top 3,000 feet per minute.

The cell becomes mature, its second stage, when precipitation starts reaching the ground. As rain or hail falls, it pulls the surrounding air down with it and builds a strong downdraft, a column of sinking air. It sits right beside the updraft.
The ground stops that sinking air, so it spreads out sideways along the surface. This spreading air is the outflow, cool and gusty, and it gets well out ahead of the cell that made it.
The weather is at its worst late in the mature stage, the same stage that sends the outflow out. A single cell's whole life cycle is typically about 30 minutes.

article.heading: What the gust front is
paragraphs: Picture the storm from above, and the outflow fans out across the ground from under the cell. Its front edge forms an arc, bowed out ahead of the storm.
That arc is the gust front, the front line of the cool air the storm has pushed out. The handbook likens it to a small cold front, and its glossary says it may also be called an outflow boundary.

The comparison fits. A gust front is the edge of a body of cool air shoving into the air ahead, and air gets lifted along that edge. That lift can set off new cells, sometimes well ahead of the one that made the outflow.
The handbook puts no number on how far ahead the gust front runs. Well ahead is as precise as it gets, so there's no mileage in it to treat as a safe margin.

figure.caption: From above, the gust front bows out ahead of the cell, so a track that misses the cloud can still cross the outflow.
figure.alt: From above, the gust front bows out ahead of the cell, so a track that misses the cloud can still cross the outflow.

article.heading: What the gust front can look like
paragraphs: Sometimes a gust front brings a low cloud along its edge, which gives you something to see. The handbook names two, the shelf cloud and the roll cloud.
A shelf cloud is a low wedge of cloud lying level, still joined to the base of the storm cloud above it. It's the more familiar of the two.
A roll cloud is a low tube of cloud lying on its side. It sits completely apart from the storm's base, and that gap is what tells it from a shelf cloud. Roll clouds are relatively rare.
The word that matters here is sometimes. A gust front doesn't always bring either cloud, so clear air ahead of a storm doesn't show you where its wind stops.

figure.caption: A shelf cloud stays joined to the storm's base, while a roll cloud floats free of it and is the rarer sight.
figure.alt: A shelf cloud stays joined to the storm's base, while a roll cloud floats free of it and is the rarer sight.

article.heading: Why you can't judge the outflow by eye
paragraphs: Not every thunderstorm holds every hazard, but the handbook says you can't tell which ones a storm holds by looking. The handbook's list of storm hazards includes adverse winds and turbulence.
So don't read a missing rain shaft as a missing outflow. The life cycle explains where a downdraft comes from. It isn't a test you can run by eye from a distance.

A dying cell isn't harmless either. Its last stage, called dissipating, is marked by a strong downdraft inside the area of rain. Sinking air takes over the whole cloud, and the rain tapers off and ends.
The handbook also warns that rain and dust between the cloud base and the ground can cut visibility. And the outflow spreads along the surface, so it's the air you fly through close to the ground.
The handbook's rule is to treat any weather you recognize as a thunderstorm as hazardous. With the outflow in mind, that has to mean the storm's wind as well as its cloud.

article.heading: How the gust front can shift a storm
paragraphs: The handbook asks you to think of a thunderstorm as something happening, not a thing parked in the sky. Air rises, rains out and sinks, while cells form and die.
Almost all storms are multicell, a cluster of cells at different stages of life. A cluster can last several hours or more, so the 30 minutes belongs to one cell and not the storm.

A storm moves in two ways at once. Its cells drift with the average wind through the depth of the cloud, which the handbook calls advection. Old cells dying and new ones forming is the other way, called propagation.

New cells set off by a gust front are part of that propagation. When one forms well ahead of the parent, the storm has spread that way without any cell drifting there. The handbook warns that storm motion can differ a lot from the motion of its cells.

posts.title: Freezing level inside a cloud layer
posts.headline: In cloud, you cross the freezing level without seeing it.
posts.alt: Freezing level inside a cloud layer: an illustrated diagram for pilots. In cloud, you cross the freezing level without seeing it. The picture shows one thick continuous cloud layer that clearly spans both above and below the freezing level; a thin dashed horizontal freezing-level line crossing through the inside of the cloud, not at its base or top; a ghost aircraft, pale and translucent, inside the cloud below the freezing line; the solid aircraft inside the same cloud, above the freezing line. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Where does the freezing level sit when you're climbing through cloud?

Structural icing needs visible moisture and an airframe at or below freezing, and a cold-soaked airframe can be below freezing in air that is not. A climb through one layer can cross the freezing level while you're still inside the cloud, with the same moisture around you. Nothing outside looks different.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Structural icing needs visible moisture and an airframe surface at or below freezing, and a cold-soaked airframe can be below freezing in air that is not.
A climb through a cloud layer can cross a freezing level inside the cloud.
Below a front, rain from warmer air above can fall into below-freezing air, become supercooled, and freeze on impact with an aircraft.
Icing in freezing precipitation often covers a broad area, and a pilot may be unable to escape it by descending.
posts.intent: Cloud and sub-zero temperature are two separate conditions, and structural ice needs both, so the climb is the decision.

article.heading: Why ice needs cloud and cold together
paragraphs: Picture a climb out through a solid overcast with the ground falling away. You are wet the whole way up, but moisture alone does not make ice.

Structural icing, the ice that builds on the outside of the airframe, needs two things at the same time. One is visible moisture, such as cloud or rain. The other is an airframe surface at or below freezing.

For the air, the handbooks are plain about it. The outside air temperature, or OAT, has to be below 0 °C for icing to happen. There is one exception, covered further down, because the airframe does not always match the air.

Ice matters because of what it does to airflow, far more than its weight. Frost or ice no rougher than coarse sandpaper on the leading edge or top of the wing can cut lift by 30 percent. That same thin layer can raise drag by up to 40 percent, and bigger buildups by 80 percent or more.

article.heading: Where the freezing level hides in cloud
paragraphs: The freezing level is the height where the air temperature passes through 0 °C. Higher air is typically colder, which is why the handbooks list temperature and altitude together.
A cloud layer does not stop at the freezing level. One layer can straddle it, with its lower part in air above zero and its upper part in air below.
Climb through that layer and you cross the line while still inside the cloud. The moisture around you is the same before and after. Only the temperature changed, and the cloud gives no sign of it.
That makes the climb itself the decision. Below the line, the cloud supplies moisture and the air is above freezing. Above it, the cloud supplies both ingredients at once.

article.heading: How cold the icing band usually is
paragraphs: Passing 0 °C does not mean more ice with every degree. Clouds hold supercooled water, liquid drops colder than freezing, and the colder the cloud gets, the less of it there is. Eventually only ice crystals remain.
That is why icing bunches into a band of temperature and height. High stratiform cloud colder than -20 °C is mostly ice crystals and gives little icing. The table shows where the reports gather.

Temperature also shapes the kind of ice. Rime, the rough milky kind, tends to form colder than -15 °C, and mixed ice forms between that and -10 °C. Clear ice, glossy and hard to see, tends to form warmer than -10 °C.
So the first degrees past the freezing level are clear ice territory. The handbooks call this general guidance, since drop size, water content and the aircraft itself change the result.

table.caption: Where icing reports cluster, as FAA-H-8083-28 and AC 00-6B give them
rows: The only physical cold limit, where liquid drops freeze on their own

article.heading: When the airframe is colder than the air
paragraphs: Say you have been flying in cold air and then descend into air above 0 °C. The airframe does not warm up to the air temperature straight away.
This is called cold soaking. A cold-soaked airframe can stay below 0 °C for some time, and on some aircraft it stays that cold even after landing.
Aircraft with fuel tanks mounted flush to the skin are especially prone to this. They can pick up ice in air only slightly above 0 °C.
So an OAT reading just above zero is not a clean bill of health in cloud. How long an airframe holds the cold varies from type to type, so know your own aircraft's limits.

article.heading: Why the top of a layer ices most
paragraphs: Flat, layered cloud is called stratiform. In low and middle stratiform layers, icing on average sits in a band 3,000 to 4,000 ft thick, and it usually runs from trace to light.
The strongest icing in these layers is in the upper part of the cloud. In a climb where the freezing level sits mid-layer, that upper part is exactly where you arrive after crossing it.
The shallow band helps you. A change of only a few thousand feet may take you out of the icing, even while you stay in cloud. The catch is that these layers spread a very long way sideways.

Heaped cloud, called cumuliform, is built differently. Its icing is narrower but taller, and in a building cloud it runs through every level above the freezing level. It is worst near the top, where the updraft is concentrated.

article.heading: When descending does not get you out
paragraphs: Going down to warmer air has a trap near fronts, which is where most icing reports come from. Under a front, air above freezing can sit on top of a layer below freezing.
Rain forms up in the warm air and falls into the cold layer underneath. The drops cool below freezing but stay liquid, which makes them supercooled. They freeze the moment they strike an aircraft.

This is a favoured spot for severe clear icing, because there is so much supercooled water. If the cold layer is shallow, the rain reaches the ground as freezing rain. If it is deep, the drops freeze into ice pellets, and ice pellets mean icing above.
Freezing rain often covers a broad area. With the cold air underneath you, a pilot may be unable to escape it by descending.

figure.caption: Rain made in the warm air above the front turns supercooled in the cold wedge below it, and that wedge is where the aircraft is.
figure.alt: Rain made in the warm air above the front turns supercooled in the cold wedge below it, and that wedge is where the aircraft is.

article.heading: What to do when ice starts
paragraphs: Whatever ice protection your aircraft has, the first move is to leave the visible moisture. That could mean descending below the cloud bases, climbing above the tops, or turning onto a different course.
If none of those is possible, move to an altitude where the temperature is above freezing. Under freezing rain that may not work, and near mountains the terrain may stop you from descending to it.
Ice also feeds itself once it starts. Adding power and raising the nose to hold altitude increases the angle of attack, and that lets ice collect on the underside of the wings and fuselage.

posts.title: Carburettor ice on a warm day
posts.headline: Your carburettor makes its own cold, whatever the OAT.
posts.alt: Carburettor ice on a warm day: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Your carburettor makes its own cold, whatever the OAT. The picture shows a rendered single-engine aeroplane in level cruise, small and high in the frame, over hazy summer farmland; a large cutaway of its carburettor filling the near foreground, sectioned along the induction path so intake mouth, venturi throat and throttle plate all read; pale streamlines entering the intake mouth and squeezing through the narrow throat, with the fuel spray leaving the nozzle in that same throat; a granular rime collar around the partly closed throttle plate, feathering thinner up the bore wall behind it. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: How does carburettor ice form when the outside air is well above freezing?

Fuel vaporising in the venturi absorbs heat, and the pressure drop through it cools the induction air further. The charge can end up below freezing. A warm OAT is what makes the risk easy to dismiss, and reduced power in humid air is when it shows up.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Fuel vaporisation and the pressure drop through the venturi cool the induction air substantially below ambient.
Carburettor ice is therefore possible at outside air temperatures well above freezing, particularly at high humidity and reduced power.
posts.intent: The temperature drop happens inside the carburettor, so ice forms on a day well above freezing.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 7

figure_key.label: COLDER THAN OUTSIDE AIR
figure_key.points_at: The narrow venturi throat, at the point the fuel spray leaves the nozzle.

figure_key.label: ICE NARROWING THE GAP
figure_key.points_at: The rime collar on the partly closed throttle plate and the shrunken air gap past it.

figure_key.label: PLATE OPEN, BORE CLEAR
figure_key.points_at: The ghost cutaway's wide-open throttle plate and clean bore.

article.heading: Where the cold comes from
paragraphs: Start with a warm, humid day and a float-type carburettor, the more common type and the one small aircraft usually carry. It is named for a float that rests on the fuel in its float chamber, the bowl that feeds the carburettor. Outside air passes through a filter, usually at the front of the cowling, and enters through the air inlet.

Inside, the air passes through the venturi, a narrow throat in the carburettor. The venturi's shape creates an area of low pressure. Fuel in the float chamber sits at higher pressure, so it is pushed out of the discharge nozzle into that throat.

Two things now cool the air. Its pressure has dropped, and the fuel is turning from liquid to vapour, which is called vaporisation. Together they make a sharp temperature drop right inside the carburettor.

The discharge nozzle must sit at the venturi throat, where the pressure is low. The throttle valve, worked by the throttle in the cockpit, sits on the engine side of the nozzle. So the fuel cools the air inside the venturi, and ice forms readily there and on the throttle valve.

A pressure-type carburettor, rarely found on small aircraft, sprays fuel under pressure on the engine side of the throttle valve. There, engine heat offsets the cooling, and the risk of fuel vaporisation icing almost disappears.

figure.caption: Fuel enters at the venturi throat, ahead of the throttle valve, which is why ice collects in both places.
figure.alt: Fuel enters at the venturi throat, ahead of the throttle valve, which is why ice collects in both places.

article.heading: How much colder the carburettor gets
paragraphs: The FAA's Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25, chapter 7) puts the temperature drop at as much as 60 to 70 Fahrenheit degrees. Read that as a difference on the scale, not a temperature of 70 °F.
Converting a difference takes care. Water freezes and boils 180 degrees apart in Fahrenheit and 100 degrees apart in Celsius. So a drop of 70 Fahrenheit degrees is 38.89 Celsius degrees.

Now run the handbook's own example. Air at 100 °F (38 °C) that loses 70 Fahrenheit degrees is at 30 °F (-1 °C) inside the carburettor. That carburettor air is below freezing, 32 °F (0 °C), on a day you would call hot.
The FAA's weather handbook, AC 00-6B, gives a similar figure. It says carburetion, the mixing of fuel and air, can cool the incoming air by as much as 33 °C.

figure.caption: On the handbook's 100 °F day, a 70-degree drop leaves the carburettor air below the freezing line.
figure.alt: On the handbook's 100 °F day, a 70-degree drop leaves the carburettor air below the freezing line.

article.heading: Why a warm day is no protection
paragraphs: Cold air on its own makes no ice. Water vapour, the water carried invisibly in the air, has to condense into liquid while the carburettor is at or below freezing. When it does, ice may form on the surfaces inside, the throttle valve among them.
So the day's moisture matters too. Relative humidity tells you how close the air is to saturation, the point where it can hold no more water vapour. At 100 percent the air is saturated.

The Pilot's Handbook rates ice most likely below 70 °F (21 °C) with relative humidity above 80 percent. Because the cooling is so sharp, it also says icing can happen with outside air as hot as 100 °F (38 °C). Humidity on such a day can be as low as 50 percent.
The weather handbook agrees. It says ice can form even under clear skies, with outside air as warm as 33 °C (90 °F) and relative humidity of 50 percent or more.
The Pilot's Handbook charts these conditions from 20 °F (-7 °C) to 100 °F (38 °C). Its caption still warns that icing is possible in conditions the chart does not show.

table.caption: Where the two FAA handbooks place carburettor icing, by outside air temperature and relative humidity.

article.heading: Why low power raises the risk
paragraphs: The ice builds where the cold is, around the throttle valve and in the venturi throat. It narrows the path for the fuel-air mixture, and the engine loses power. If enough builds up, the engine may stop.

Reduced power makes this worse. Close the throttle in flight and the engine cools quickly, and the fuel vaporises less completely than it would in a warm engine. The Pilot's Handbook says the engine is more prone to carburettor ice in that state.
Ice can form in any phase of flight. A descent at reduced power is when it is particularly dangerous. Under some conditions it can build unnoticed there and show itself only when you add power.
Size is no comfort either. The weather handbook says even a small amount of carburettor ice costs power and may make the engine run rough.

article.heading: How you notice it forming
paragraphs: With a fixed-pitch propeller, the first sign is a drop in engine rpm. Engine roughness may follow.
A constant-speed propeller changes its own pitch to make up for lost power, so it holds rpm steady. In that aircraft, the rpm will not show the ice.
Watch manifold pressure instead, the pressure in the intake manifold that carries the mixture to the combustion chambers. Carburettor ice shows there as a falling reading while rpm stays the same.

Whichever propeller you have, you are looking for lost power, and you may see it as lost altitude or airspeed. Vibration or roughness sometimes comes with it. Once you notice the loss, act at once to clear the ice that has formed and stop more from forming.

article.heading: How carburettor heat clears the ice
paragraphs: Engines with float-type carburettors carry a carburettor heat system for this. It is an anti-icing system that warms the air before it reaches the carburettor, to keep the fuel-air mixture above freezing. It can also melt ice that has already formed, as long as there is not too much.
When you find ice, apply full heat immediately and leave it on until you are sure the ice is gone. Partial heat, or heat left on too briefly, might make things worse.

Full heat cuts power further, and the engine may run rough as melted ice passes through. That can last from 30 seconds to several minutes. Resist easing the heat back, and keep it at full hot until normal power returns.

The rpm tells you whether there was ice. With a fixed-pitch propeller and ice present, rpm drops when the heat goes on, then slowly rises as the ice melts. With no ice, rpm drops and then holds steady.
With a constant-speed propeller, ice shows as a fall in manifold pressure and then a slow rise. With no ice, you see no rise until you turn the heat off.

article.heading: Using heat before the ice arrives
paragraphs: Prevention is the better use of carburettor heat, and you check that it works during the engine runup. If you suspect icing conditions and expect to close the throttle, set full heat first. Leave it on for as long as the throttle stays closed.
Every so often during that time, open the throttle smoothly for a few seconds. That keeps the engine warm, and without it the carburettor heater may not supply enough heat to stop ice forming.

Heat has a cost. Heated air is less dense, so engine power falls, sometimes by up to 15 percent, and the mixture gets richer. Because it cuts power and raises engine temperature, keep it off for takeoff and normal running unless checking for or clearing ice.
Some aircraft carry a carburettor air temperature gauge to help you spot icing conditions. Its face usually shows a yellow arc from -15 °C to +5 °C (5 °F to 41 °F), the range where icing may occur.
When the temperature and moisture make icing unlikely, the needle can sit in the yellow without harm. When conditions favour icing, use carburettor heat to keep it out of the arc.

posts.title: Acceleration that feels like a climb
posts.headline: With nothing to see outside, speeding up feels like pitching up.
posts.alt: Acceleration that feels like a climb: an illustrated diagram for pilots. With nothing to see outside, speeding up feels like pitching up. The picture shows a rendered Cessna 172 in clean left profile, seen level and square to its flank, high wing with visible struts and fixed tricycle gear, its nose pitched clearly down below level; a translucent outline of the same aeroplane overlapping it and sharing its tail position, pitched clearly nose-high, so the picture reads as one aeroplane in two attitudes rather than as two aircraft; a wide, obvious angle between the two noses, the ghost's high and the solid one's low, which is the subject of the picture; a thin pale line tracing the aeroplane's real path: up off the runway, over a shallow crest, then bending down toward the unlit water. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Why does forward acceleration feel like a nose-up pitch attitude?

Accelerate forward with no outside references and your sense of pitch says the nose came up. It did not, and the correction it invites is lowering the nose toward the surface. Nothing outside can settle it, so fly the pitch on the flight instruments and disregard what your body is reporting.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Forward acceleration can produce a false sensation of a nose-up pitch attitude.
Without outside visual references the pilot may lower the nose toward the surface, so pitch must be flown on the flight instruments rather than on what the body reports.
posts.intent: On a dark night takeoff, acceleration pushes the inner ear the same way a nose-up pitch would, and the instinct is to push down.

article.heading: What happens on a dark night takeoff
paragraphs: Picture a night takeoff toward open water. You add full power, the aeroplane gathers speed, and the runway lights slide away behind you. Ahead of the windscreen there is nothing to look at.
Somewhere in the roll or the first part of the climb, your body tells you the nose has come up. It feels steep. The aeroplane has not pitched up at all.
The instinct that follows is to ease the stick forward and bring the nose down. That is the trap. The rest of this page walks through where the feeling comes from and why the answer is on the panel.

article.heading: Why speeding up feels like tilting back
paragraphs: Your inner ear holds the otolith organs. They are the part of your balance system that senses which way gravity and acceleration are pulling on your head.

Tilt your head backwards and the otolith organs register the change. A hard shove forward, like the one you get on a takeoff roll, stimulates them in the same way. From that signal alone, your brain cannot tell the two apart.
So it reports the familiar story. You feel yourself tilting back, which in an aeroplane means nose-up. This false sense of a raised nose from speeding up is called the somatogravic illusion.
The handbook uses takeoff as its example, because that is where a rapid acceleration is part of every flight. You meet the conditions for it every time you open the throttle.

figure.caption: Tilting your head back and speeding up forward send your inner ear the same message.
figure.alt: Tilting your head back and speeding up forward send your inner ear the same message.

article.heading: Why a dark night makes it worse
paragraphs: In daylight your eyes settle the question. You glance out, see the horizon where it should be, and know the nose is where you put it.

The illusion is most likely when visual references are poor. Over open water at night, black water meets black sky with no seam, and there is nothing to check the feeling against. The handbook names that exact case as flight without a visible horizon.
It lumps marginal visibility in with it, meaning visibility of less than 3 miles. In either case the inner ear becomes the loudest voice left in the cockpit.

Seat of the pants flying will not save you here. That means judging attitude from the pressure you feel through your seat, skin and muscles. Acceleration forces can overpower gravity, and then those signals go false as well.

article.heading: What the wrong correction does
paragraphs: Convinced the nose is high, a disoriented pilot pushes forward. The handbook says this can put the aeroplane into a nose-low attitude, or into a dive.
Just after takeoff you have very little height to give away. Lowering the nose there points the aeroplane at the surface you just left, while your body still insists you are climbing.

The illusion also runs in reverse. Pull the throttle back quickly and the rapid slowdown can have the opposite effect. The disoriented pilot then pulls the nose up, toward a nose-high attitude or a stall.

table.caption: The same sensor, fooled in both directions by a change in speed.
rows: Rapid acceleration, such as on takeoff
Pushes into a nose-low or dive attitude
Rapid deceleration from a quick throttle reduction
Pulls into a nose-up or stall attitude

article.heading: How to feel it safely with an instructor
paragraphs: You can meet this illusion on purpose. The handbook describes a demonstration called climbing while accelerating.

You close your eyes. Your instructor holds approach speed, straight and level, for several seconds. Then they speed up while keeping the aeroplane straight and level, and the usual sensation is that you are climbing.

A second exercise gets the same feeling from a turn. The instructor rolls slowly into a coordinated turn of about 1.5 positive G, approximately 50° of bank, and holds it for 90°. G is the load pressing you into your seat, and here it reads as a climb too.

Both exercises prove the same point. Your body's sense of attitude is often wrong, while the instruments are not fooled. Do them only at a safe height, with an instructor or a suitable safety pilot aboard.

article.heading: How to fly pitch on the instruments
paragraphs: Take pitch from the flight instruments, and treat what your body reports as noise. On a dark takeoff, set the attitude you want on the panel and hold it there. If the nose feels like it is climbing away, check the instruments before you touch the stick.

The false feeling is normal, and no amount of training makes it go away completely. What training does is teach you to override it. The more instrument flying you do, the less these illusions pull on you.
Get that training before you need it. The handbook says to get it before flying in visibility under 3 miles. The same goes for anywhere without a visible horizon, such as over open water at night.

Keep your head still during the takeoff, since sudden head movement is on the handbook's list of things to avoid. Arrive rested, too. Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, lost sleep and mild hypoxia, a shortage of oxygen, all make you easier to fool.

posts.title: Rotor cloud under a mountain wave
posts.headline: In a mountain wave, the roughest low-level air is under that smooth cloud.
posts.alt: Rotor cloud under a mountain wave: an illustrated diagram for pilots. In a mountain wave, the roughest low-level air is under that smooth cloud. The picture shows a mountain ridge in profile with the wind crossing it left to right; a smooth, hard-edged lens of lenticular cloud sitting at the wave crest downwind of the summit; a torn, ragged rotor cloud directly below that lenticular, at about ridge-top height; streamlines drawn unbroken from the lenticular down into the rotor, so the two clouds read as one wave. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: What's the difference between a lenticular cloud and a rotor cloud?

Air crossing a ridge can set up a standing wave downwind. Smooth lenticular cloud marks the crests. The rotor turns underneath, and down low that roll is usually the roughest part. The wave can be rough higher up too, so smooth cloud above is not a promise of smooth air.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: A mountain wave can form smooth lenticular cloud at its crests and turbulent rotor cloud beneath them.
At low level the rotor beneath the crests is usually the most turbulent part of the wave.
A mountain wave is often marked by lenticular and rotor clouds, but extremely severe wave winds can occur with little or no visual warning.

article.heading: How a ridge sets the air waving
paragraphs: Picture a strong wind blowing across a mountain ridge on a stable day. Stable air resists being lifted, because once it is pushed up it is heavier than the air around it.

After the air clears the top of the ridge, gravity pulls it back down. Momentum carries it below its starting level, and compression warms it as it sinks, until it is lighter than the air around it. Up it goes again, overshoots again, and keeps bobbing downstream until the motion dies out.
That train of rises and falls is a mountain wave, and its high points are its crests. Air climbing toward a crest cools as it expands. With enough moisture, its water vapor condenses into cloud.

The cloud at a crest is a lenticular, named for its lens or airfoil shape. Lenticulars often line up in fairly straight bands parallel to the ridge but downwind of it, with clear sky between. Each band sits on a crest, so a row of them draws the wave for you.

article.heading: What a lenticular's edges tell you
paragraphs: The edges of a wave cloud give you a clue to the air inside it. Smooth, laminar edges and tops, meaning they look sleek and layered, go with little or no turbulence.

A lumpy, uneven cloud says the opposite. So does any sense that it is rolling around an axis running along the cloud. Lenticulars themselves can look either smooth or turbulent, so read each one on its own.
A smooth-looking lenticular layer can still be rough at the bottom. Inside the layer, the air typically runs from turbulent near its base to smooth near its top.

The wave also roughens the air at its crests and at its troughs, the low points between them. It moves strong wind up and down, which sharpens the wind shear, a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a short distance. Shear like that stirs up turbulence.

article.heading: Why the air under the crest rolls
paragraphs: When a mountain wave is present, a rotor quite commonly forms on the downwind side of the mountain. A rotor is a horizontal roll of air that stays put, near or below ridge height, beneath a wave crest. With enough moisture, it shows up as a rotor cloud under the lenticular.

The rotor zone is an area of possibly severe to extreme wind shear and turbulence. Some references call shear severe when it shifts your airspeed by more than 15 kt. They also count a change in vertical speed of more than 500 feet per minute, or fpm.

The roughness comes with big changes in the wind below cloud level. Just downwind of the mountains, a strong shear layer often sits near the cloud base. It splits a turbulent wake below mountaintop height, the churned air behind the mountain, from the faster air above that carries the cloud.
The wind beneath lenticulars can swing and gust a lot, but it is usually not extremely strong. Pilots flying near these clouds often report moderate to severe turbulence underneath them.
Those cloud bases typically sit one to several thousand feet above ridge level. The rotor turns lower, near or below the ridge, and at that level it is usually the most turbulent part of the wave.

article.heading: Where the downslope windstorm ends
paragraphs: Rotors typically sit at the far end of a downslope windstorm. That is strong wind racing down the lee slope, the downwind side of the mountain, after the wave breaks high above. Gusts on those slopes can reach 100 kt.

That fast flow does not fade out gently. It often stops abruptly, some distance down the lee slope or well downwind of the mountains, and that stopping place is called the jump. When a rotor marks the end of the windstorm, it belongs to the jump itself.

Extreme turbulence often fills the jump, stretching 10,000 ft or more above the ground. A line of ragged rotor clouds sometimes marks it. Beyond the jump the air calms somewhat, but the turbulence can still be strong.

figure.caption: The rotor line sits over the jump, where the fast wind down the lee slope ends and extreme turbulence is frequent.
figure.alt: The rotor line sits over the jump, where the fast wind down the lee slope ends and extreme turbulence is frequent.

article.heading: How to spot a rotor cloud early
paragraphs: A rotor and its cloud are usually spinning hard. From a moving airplane, though, you may not see the spin until you are quite close.
From far off, a rotor cloud can pass for a harmless cumulus, the billowy cloud of a sunny afternoon. Look at its downwind side. It is typically rounded in the direction the rotor turns.
Then look along the bottom for ragged tags or streamers of cloud. They seem to form and vanish quickly, and that flicker is what gives you a sense of the spin inside.

article.heading: What a rotor does to your airplane
paragraphs: The advice on rotor zones is to stay out of them. Strong turbulence is likely around a rotor, most of all on its upwind side.
The spinning air can also produce rolling moments, forces that bank the airplane, stronger than your controls can counter. That can end in a loss of control.
Low altitude is where a rotor is most dangerous, and takeoff and landing top the list. You are slow then, and the airplane is set up for relatively high drag.

Close to the runway in mountain winds, local gusts above 50 kt are possible, with downdrafts greater than 1,500 fpm. A downdraft can sink you faster than your airplane can climb. Airplanes with high wing and power loading, meaning lots of weight for their wing and engine, are most exposed.

rows: Suspect disturbances downwind of rugged terrain
10,000 ft or more above the surface

article.heading: When the wave leaves no clouds
paragraphs: Lenticulars and rotor clouds need enough moisture in the air arriving at the mountain. Mountain waves often come with them, or with blowing dust. That is not always so, and extremely severe winds can arrive with little or no visual warning.
So a clear sky downwind of a ridge does not mean there is no wave. Trapped lee waves, waves whose energy stays below a certain height, frequently occur without any cloud.

Watch the wind instead. Suspect hidden disturbances whenever you fly downwind of rugged terrain with ridge-level wind above about 20 kt. That figure is the prevailing wind at the ridge crest, upwind of you, not a local gust.

Fly low over mountains with 20 kt or more at ridge level and you can expect moderate or greater turbulence. You can also expect strong updrafts and downdrafts, and very strong rotor and shear zones. That holds most of all for general aviation airplanes, the kind you likely train in.

The worst mountain wind events tend to fall between late autumn and early spring, when the big weather-map winds blow hardest. In a wave flow, fly at turbulence penetration speed, the speed meant for rough air. Stay clear of terrain that drops away sharply, even with no lenticular in sight.

posts.headline: Usable fuel is less than your tanks hold.

article.heading: What a full tank does not tell you
paragraphs: You fill the tanks to the top of the filler neck and cap them. The number printed on the tank, or on the fuel gauge placard, is the total the tanks hold. Some of that fuel will never reach the engine.

That leftover share is called unusable fuel, the fuel that stays in the tanks and lines and cannot be relied on in flight. Whatever is left after you take it away is usable fuel, the fuel the engine can actually burn.

Pilots often treat the gap between the two as a rounding error. It is not. The manufacturer measures it and publishes it for your aircraft type. A full tank tells you what you carry, and the usable figure tells you what you can burn.

article.heading: Why some fuel never reaches the engine
paragraphs: Fuel has a long way to travel before it burns. In a fuel-injected engine it leaves the tank and passes through an engine-driven fuel pump. Then it goes to a fuel-air control unit, which does the job a carburetor would do.

From there the fuel runs to a fuel manifold, the valve that splits it between cylinders. Discharge nozzles in each cylinder head then spray it into the intake ports. An auxiliary fuel pump backs up the engine-driven pump for starting and emergencies.

The whole chain draws from the tank through an outlet called the pickup. Fuel lying below that outlet, or trapped in the shape of the tank floor, cannot be drawn into the lines. It is still fuel, and it still shows as part of the total, but the engine cannot use it.

article.heading: Where the usable number comes from
paragraphs: You do not work out unusable fuel yourself. The manufacturer establishes it, and it is written in the approved flight manual for your aircraft. That manual is called the airplane flight manual (AFM) or the pilot's operating handbook (POH).

This is the same place the manufacturer publishes other limits you must respect. The fore and aft limits for the center of gravity, the balance point of the loaded aircraft, sit in the AFM or POH. They also appear in the Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS), the aircraft's official specification.

Look in the fuel section of your AFM or POH. You will find total capacity and usable capacity listed as separate figures. Two aircraft that look alike on the ramp can carry different numbers, so read the manual for the one you are flying.

article.heading: What the unusable fuel still costs you
paragraphs: Unusable fuel gives you no range, but it does not weigh nothing. Gasoline weighs 6 pounds per gallon. Every gallon trapped in the tank is 6 pounds you carry for the whole flight.

Weight matters because too much of it hurts nearly every part of performance. An overloaded aircraft needs a longer takeoff run and climbs more slowly. It also stalls at a higher speed and needs a longer landing roll.

During a flight, burning fuel is normally the only change in weight. As the usable fuel goes, the aircraft gets lighter and performs better. The unusable fuel stays aboard, so it counts as weight from engine start to shutdown.

Where fuel sits also affects balance. If you feed the engine unevenly from tanks on one side, the aircraft becomes wing-heavy. Holding it level with trim or control pressure adds drag and wastes fuel you had planned to use.

article.heading: What happens when the plan uses total fuel
paragraphs: Picture two plans for the same trip. One divides the total capacity by the fuel burn. The other divides the usable capacity. The first plan promises you minutes of flight that the tanks cannot deliver.

When the usable fuel runs out, the engine stops getting fuel even though the tanks are not dry. That is fuel starvation, the engine quitting because fuel no longer reaches it. The gauge and the tank may both suggest fuel is still aboard.

Restarting is not a sure thing either. Fuel-injected engines have a known weakness here. Restarting one that quit from fuel starvation brings its own problems, so an engine that stops this way does not reliably come back.

article.heading: How to plan from the usable figure
paragraphs: Start every fuel calculation with the usable capacity from the AFM or POH, never the total. If the tanks are not full, work out how much usable fuel is actually aboard. Only that quantity goes into your time and range sums.

Treat the usable figure as a ceiling, not a target. Your plan should land with fuel still in the tanks, including the reserve the regulations require. Those reserve rules come from the regulations, and the source here does not give their figures.

Carrying less fuel to save weight is a fair choice, but it trades away range. If you remove fuel to get under a weight limit, redo the fuel plan with the smaller usable quantity. Then check the new figure still covers the trip and the reserve.

posts.title: Ground effect in the flare
posts.headline: Your drag falls away inside the last wingspan.
posts.alt: Ground effect in the flare: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Your drag falls away inside the last wingspan. The picture shows a rendered light single nose-high in the flare, wings level, main wheels hovering a few feet above the runway centreline; a ticked vertical dimension line one wingspan tall from the low aircraft's wingtip to the asphalt, with the aeroplane sitting well inside it; ghost comparison: the same aeroplane in the same nose-high attitude, a pale unfilled outline about one and a half wingspans higher and slightly behind; tip trails behind the low aircraft pressed wide and shallow along the asphalt, while the ghost's trails curl into two deep, tight vortices. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Throttle closed, the nose where you set it, and the airplane keeps flying down the runway.
Come within a wingspan of the surface and the wing enters ground effect. Induced drag goes down. The airplane holds off, and the runway keeps going by.
The same thing happens on takeoff. You can be airborne below normal flying speed, then settle back as you climb out of the last wingspan.
FlightDecide computes your takeoff weight from the fuel you loaded.
Full explainer with the FAA sources it rests on https://flightdecide.com/explainers/ground-effect-in-the-flare/
When somebody asks why you floated, what is the one word in your answer?
teaches: Within about one wingspan of the surface, ground effect reduces induced drag and the thrust required to hold a low airspeed in level flight.
The reduced drag is why an aircraft floats in the flare and why it can lift off below normal flying speed and settle back.
posts.intent: Within about one wingspan of the surface induced drag falls away, so the aeroplane floats on air that has nowhere to go.
