article.heading: What you feel just before touchdown
paragraphs: You've closed the throttle and eased the nose up for the flare, the gentle pitch-up just before touchdown. Now you're waiting for the wheels to touch, but the runway keeps sliding past and the airplane keeps flying just above it. It doesn't seem to want to come down.

Pilots have noticed this since the first flights, and it feels like a cushion of air trapped under the wing. Its name is ground effect, the change in airflow around an airplane flying close to the ground or water.

Ground effect normally reaches up to about one wingspan above the surface. Inside that height the wing loses part of its induced drag, the drag that comes with making lift. With less drag to slow it, the airplane gives up its speed slowly and floats.

article.heading: Where induced drag comes from
paragraphs: A wing holds the airplane up by pushing air downward. The air streaming down behind the wing is called downwash, and the harder the wing works, the more of it there is.

The air under the wing is at higher pressure than the air above it. Near each tip it flows sideways around the edge and rolls up into a spinning tube called a wingtip vortex. Making the downwash and the vortices takes energy, and that energy is paid for as induced drag.

Slow flight makes it worse. To hold the airplane up at lower speed you need a higher angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the oncoming air. A higher angle means a bigger pressure difference, stronger vortices and more induced drag.

Induced drag rises as the inverse square of airspeed, so slowing down makes it grow fast. At high speed, parasite drag, the drag of moving the airframe itself through the air, makes up most of the total. In the flare you are slow, so induced drag is the part that dominates.

article.heading: What the runway does to the airflow
paragraphs: Now bring that wing down near the runway. The air it pushes down has nowhere to go, because the surface blocks its path downward. The ground is interfering with the airflow, and that interference is ground effect.
That blocked flow weakens the upwash, the air rising to meet the front of the wing. It weakens the downwash behind the wing and the wingtip vortices too.

Smaller vortices change how lift is spread along the span, and induced drag falls. The wing now needs a lower angle of attack to make the same lift. Hold the old angle and it makes more lift than it did.

article.heading: How close the wing has to be
paragraphs: As you descend through that last wingspan, ground effect grows, and most of it arrives very close to the runway. The Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge gives the figures.
With the wing one wingspan above the ground, induced drag drops by only 1.4 percent. At 1/4 of the span the drop is 23.5 percent. At 1/10 of the span it is 47.6 percent, close to half.
The Airplane Flying Handbook rounds those two lower figures to about 25 percent and about 50 percent. Either way, the big saving only comes with the wing very near the surface.

So one wingspan marks where ground effect can first be detected, and the lower heights show where it does real work. Because the saving sits so low, you notice it most just after lift-off and just before touchdown.

figure.caption: Induced drag barely changes at one wingspan up, but nearly half of it is gone by 1/10 of the span.
figure.alt: Induced drag barely changes at one wingspan up, but nearly half of it is gone by 1/10 of the span.

article.heading: Why extra speed becomes a long float
paragraphs: Back in the flare, you hold a steady nose-up attitude at low speed, just off the runway. Those are exactly the conditions where ground effect is strongest.
Thrust required, the push needed to hold a speed in level flight, is parasite drag and induced drag added together. Ground effect cuts the induced part, so thrust required drops sharply at low speed.

With the power off, drag is what slows you down. Take a big share of it away and the airplane loses speed slowly. Any extra speed you carry into the flare can then become a long float down the runway.
The lift changes too. If the wing arrives in ground effect at the same angle of attack, it makes more lift and the airplane can float.
So as you near the ground at the end of the approach, you take some power off. Leave it in and the airplane will tend to climb.

article.heading: Why a slow lift-off can settle back
paragraphs: On takeoff the same physics runs the other way. The roll, the lift-off and the start of the climb all happen inside ground effect, where induced drag is reduced. That can make the airplane seem ready to fly well below its recommended takeoff speed.

Your instruments read differently here too. Ground effect usually raises the pressure at the static source, the port that feeds the airspeed indicator and altimeter, so both read slightly low. You can be airborne at an indicated airspeed below the one normally needed.

Climb out of ground effect and all of this reverses. The wing needs a higher angle of attack for the same lift, and induced drag and thrust required both rise. The nose tends to pitch up, stability decreases, and the airspeed indicator reads higher as static pressure falls.

If you lifted off short of speed, that extra drag arrives as you leave ground effect. Your climb will be much weaker than at Vy, the best rate of climb speed, or even Vx, the best angle of climb speed.

The worst case is a heavy airplane on a hot day at high density altitude, where the air is thin. There the airplane can lift off yet be unable to climb out of ground effect and settle back onto the runway. So you never force it into the air before the manufacturer's recommended takeoff speed.

article.heading: Using ground effect on purpose
paragraphs: Ground effect also has its uses. With a long enough runway or no obstacles, the reduced drag can help the airplane accelerate after lift-off.

A soft-field takeoff is built around it. Tall grass, soft sand, mud and snow drag at the wheels, so you hold the nose high and let the wing lift the airplane off early. It leaves the ground below a safe climb speed, held up by ground effect.

Once airborne, you lower the nose gently and let it accelerate with the wheels just clear of the surface. If it rises out of ground effect too soon, it tends to settle back even at full power. So you keep it in ground effect until it reaches at least Vx.

Some airplanes tend to lift off well before Vx on a short field. It is better to let one lift off and hold it level, wheels just clear, until it reaches Vx. Pinning it to the runway with forward pressure overloads the nosewheel and slows the acceleration.

posts.title: A narrow runway and a low approach
posts.headline: A narrow runway hides how low you really are.
posts.alt: A narrow runway and a low approach: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A narrow runway hides how low you really are. The picture shows the runway seen obliquely ahead, its paved width visibly narrow with the edges close together and the markings small and crowded; a pale unfilled outline of the usual, wider runway drawn around the real one, so the gap between true edge and outline can be read; ghost outline of the same aeroplane on the normal approach path, at the same distance out and clearly above the solid one; solid aeroplane low on a shallower path, sitting close to the ground short of the threshold. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: You're on short final at a field you've never used, and the picture out the windscreen looks normal.

The runway ahead is narrower than the ones you learned on. A runway narrower than usual creates the illusion of extra height. That is the narrow runway illusion, and it needs nothing more than the width you're looking at. The picture says come down.

Miss it and the approach goes low. Objects along the approach path start to matter, and landing short is the other end of the same mistake. The Aeronautical Information Manual files it at 8-1-5, with the rest of the illusions of flight.
FlightDecide reads the NOTAMs for your destination and flags runway and obstruction notices in the briefing.
Next time you brief an unfamiliar field, look up its runway width and compare it to your home runway.
Check the current CFR before you apply this to a real flight.
teaches: A runway narrower than usual creates the illusion that the aircraft is higher than it actually is.
A pilot who does not recognise the illusion flies a lower-than-normal approach, with the risk of striking objects along the approach path or landing short.
posts.intent: A narrower runway than you are used to makes you feel higher than you are, and the uncorrected result is an approach that is too low.

article.heading: What a narrow runway does to your eyes
paragraphs: Most of your landings have been at one airport, on one runway. Today you're on final somewhere new, and the strip ahead is clearly narrower than the one you know.
A runway narrower than you're used to can make you feel higher above the ground than you really are. The FAA calls this the runway width illusion.

The FAA's Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge says the effect is strongest when the two runways' length-to-width relationships are comparable. Nothing about the view looks wrong. It just tells you that you have height to spare.

article.heading: Why feeling high makes you fly low
paragraphs: If you think you're high, you fix it the way you were taught. The Airplane Flying Handbook says you steepen an approach that looks too high by cutting power and lowering the nose.
Except you weren't high. Once you've corrected for height you never had, you're on a lower-than-normal approach path, the line your aeroplane is really flying down toward the runway.

The AIM is firm about the outcome. A pilot who doesn't recognise the illusion will fly a lower approach. The word that matters is recognise, because the pilots it catches are the ones who aren't expecting it.

article.heading: What a low approach puts in your way
paragraphs: A low path brings you closer to everything short of the runway. The AIM names two risks. You can hit objects along the approach path, or you can land short, touching down before the runway begins.

If you find yourself low and undershooting, the handbook says to raise the nose and add power to level off, holding the correct airspeed. When you reach the glide path you want, reduce power and lower the nose to stay on it.

Trying to stretch the approach by raising the nose without adding power is almost always a bad idea, the handbook warns. If you're very low, you may not manage a stabilized approach at all, meaning one flown at a constant angle toward a chosen point. Then the normal answer is a go-around.

article.heading: A wide runway fools you the other way
paragraphs: The same illusion runs in reverse. A runway wider than you're used to can make you feel lower than you are.
The FAA's runway illusion figure says this leads to a higher approach. The AIM lists what goes wrong next. You may level off too high and land hard, or overshoot the runway.
Knowing both directions helps. Every new airport gets measured against your home runway, whether you want it to or not.

rows: Striking objects along the approach path, or landing short
Levelling out high and landing hard, or overshooting the runway

article.heading: How to read the runway picture
paragraphs: Start with the aiming point, the spot on the ground your aeroplane is heading straight for. On a steady descent it seems to stay put. It doesn't slide under the nose, and it doesn't creep away ahead of you.

Keep an eye on the gap between the aiming point and the horizon. At a constant angle that gap stays the same. If the aiming point rises toward the horizon, the point you'll really reach is closer than you think.

The runway's shape gives clues too. From final it looks like a trapezoid, and on a stabilized approach it keeps the same shape as it grows. A shallower approach makes it look shorter and wider. A steeper one makes it look longer and narrower.

Don't stare at one spot. The handbook suggests scanning from the aiming point to the horizon, to objects along the runway, to an area well short of it, and back again. It's easier to spot a drift off the path when your eyes keep moving.

figure.caption: As the approach angle changes, the runway's outline changes too, so a runway that's getting shorter and wider means your path is getting shallower.
figure.alt: As the approach angle changes, the runway's outline changes too, so a runway that's getting shorter and wider means your path is getting shallower.

article.heading: Cross-checks that don't depend on width
paragraphs: Expect illusions before you arrive at an unfamiliar airport, especially at night or in bad weather. Look at the airport diagram and the Chart Supplement U.S., the FAA's airport directory, for runway slope, terrain and lighting. If you can, look the airport over from the air before you land.

On every approach, day or night, check the altimeter often. Use a Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI) or Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI) whenever one is there. Both are lighting systems that give you a visual reference for the descent.

On an instrument approach, use the electronic glideslope if there is one. On nonprecision approaches, use the visual descent point (VDP) printed on many charts. None of these depends on how wide the runway looks.
Watch out for distraction as well. The handbook says the chance of an approach accident goes up when an emergency or some other task pulls you away from your usual routine.

posts.title: The black hole approach
posts.headline: Over dark ground you fly lower than you think.
posts.alt: The black hole approach: an illustrated diagram for pilots. With nothing lit below, you fly lower than intended. The picture shows night side elevation with the lit runway small and far in the right third and the approach entering from the left; solid aeroplane on the lower, shallower path, visibly close to the dark surface short of the field; ghost outline of the same aeroplane on the intended path at the same distance out, clearly above the solid one; completely unlit ground or water between the aeroplane and the threshold, with no towns, roads or scattered lights. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: You turn final over the bay, and the only lights anywhere are the ones on the runway.

Night approaches over unlit terrain or water have a name. The black hole approach. The cues you use to judge height and distance are gone. No roads or rooflines under the nose. Only the runway lights, sitting out there alone.

On a lit approach the picture corrects you the whole way down. Over black ground it never updates. A small sink goes unchallenged. The Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge files it with the visual illusions in chapter 17.
FlightDecide reads your destination NOTAMs for the planned window, runway lighting outages included.
If the ground below the approach shows nothing, what is left to tell you how high you are?
teaches: An approach over unlit terrain or water removes the visual cues normally used to judge height and distance.
With no surrounding ground features, the aircraft can seem higher than it actually is.
The result tends toward an approach lower than intended.
In the worst case, the aircraft lands short of the runway.
Bright runway lights with few lights around them can do the opposite, making the runway seem closer and leading to a higher approach.
posts.intent: With no lit features between you and the runway there is no visual slope information, so the approach is flown on an impression.

article.heading: What a dark final looks like
paragraphs: Picture a night approach to a runway on the shore, with the whole final leg over open water. Ahead are two lines of edge lights and a row of threshold lights. Below and around you, nothing is lit at all.

On a daytime approach you judge height from many small clues. Fields, trees, roads and buildings grow larger as you descend and slide past the edge of your view. Over black water or unlit ground, every one of those clues is gone.
Nothing about the scene feels alarming. The runway looks clear and bright, and the approach seems easy.
This is the black hole approach. It happens when you land from over water or unlit terrain and the runway lights are the only source of light.

article.heading: Why you feel higher than you are
paragraphs: Normally the ground around the runway helps you judge how high you are and how far you have to go. Part of that comes from peripheral cues, the things you notice at the edge of your vision.

Without those cues, the handbook says, orientation is difficult. Your eyes still hand you an answer, and it tends to be wrong. With nothing around the runway to compare against, the airplane seems higher than it actually is.
Water is the classic case, but it is not the only one. Unlit land does the same, and so does terrain left blank by snow. What matters is that there is nothing on the ground to read.
The runway itself can look out of place as well. It can seem to slope down away from you, or slope up toward you.

article.heading: How that ends up short of the runway
paragraphs: When the picture tells you that you are high, you correct for it by descending. The correction feels right, because it makes the view look the way you expect.
The result is an approach lower than you meant to fly. From the seat nothing looks wrong, because the error is in the picture you are flying by.
Over water or unlit land there is nothing between you and the threshold to warn you. In the worst case, the airplane lands short of the runway.
Your eyes are not failing here. They are doing their normal job with far too little to work on, so the approach ends up flown on an impression.

article.heading: When bright runway lights push you high
paragraphs: The lights around a runway can bend the error the other way. Picture a runway with bright edge and approach lights, and very few lights on the ground around it.

Bright lights make a runway look closer than it is. The handbook says this setup can create the illusion of being lower, or of having less distance to go. A pilot who misses it tends to fly a higher approach.
Now change the ground under you. Flying over terrain with only a few lights makes the runway seem to recede, or look farther away. Here the tendency is a lower than normal approach.

A city in the distance on higher ground beyond the runway also tends to pull you low. So the same dark night can push you high or low, depending on what is lit in front of you. Neither error is safe to assume.

Aircraft seems higher than it actually is
Terrain with only a few lights

article.heading: Where to expect it
paragraphs: The classic setting is an airport by the water, approached from over the water at night. The handbook also points to airports in sparsely populated areas, where there are few if any surface references.
A missing horizon or surface reference is common over water, at night and in low visibility. When all three stack up on one final, you have the conditions for this illusion.
Airports you have never flown into deserve the most suspicion. Go in expecting to be fooled, especially at night or in poor weather.

Before the flight, read the airport diagram and the Chart Supplement, which used to be called the Airport/Facility Directory. Both tell you about runway slope, the terrain around the field and the lighting. Knowing the layout and boundaries before you start down helps you hold a safe approach angle.

article.heading: What to fly by instead of the view
paragraphs: Since the view is what misleads you, judge the slope with something that does not depend on it. If there is an electronic glide slope, a descent path you follow on your instruments rather than by eye, use it.

If the runway has a visual approach slope indicator, or VASI, use that as well. It is a lighting aid at the runway that gives you a visual reference for the slope, and the handbook says to use it whenever one is available.

Where neither exists, your flight instruments help you keep your orientation and fly a normal approach. The handbook's wider advice on illusions is to rely on the instruments over what your senses report.
If at any point you doubt your altitude or your position relative to the runway, do not press on. The handbook's instruction is to go around.
Practice is part of it too. The handbook recommends keeping night currency and proficiency, flying both cross-country and local operations at a range of airfields.

posts.title: Attention narrowing under fatigue
posts.headline: Fatigue narrows your scan before you feel impaired.
posts.alt: Attention narrowing under fatigue: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Fatigue narrows your scan before you feel impaired. The picture shows side elevation of a single-engine aeroplane in profile left of centre, late in the day, with layered ridgelines stepping back to the right into haze; a narrow pale-edged cone of attention opening forward from the cockpit, reaching only one small lit notch of rock at the shoulder of the pass; ghost comparison: a thin unfilled outline of a far wider cone from the same point, spanning nearly the whole forward view, the scan the pilot believes is being flown; terrain inside the narrow cone crisp and readable, everything between its edges and the ghost outline dimmed and softened into haze. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Fourth hour in the airplane, you copy a squawk code and look up to find the heading off the bug.

Fatigue does that. It degrades attention, and it takes away the ability to divide attention between two jobs. Whatever your hands are doing wins. The instrument you were watching a minute ago goes unwatched, and nothing announces it.

You can't feel the narrowing while it's happening. Chapter 2 of the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge covers why fitness gets judged against a written checklist. The same tired brain does the self-assessment, and it reports back that everything is fine.
FlightDecide reads the TAFs and NOTAMs across your whole planned window, so late-day workload is visible early.
On a long day, the checklist is the only honest opinion in the cockpit.
teaches: Fatigue degrades attention and the ability to divide it between tasks.
Fatigue is hard to judge from how you feel: a pilot who has flown 16 hours may still say they are not too tired, so the IMSAFE checklist helps identify it.
posts.intent: Fatigue narrows the field of attention before it feels like impairment, so the scan stops covering what you think it covers.

article.heading: What fatigue takes from your attention
paragraphs: Picture the last leg of a long day. You're holding altitude and the radio calls go out on time. Nothing feels wrong, so you assume your attention is where it always is.
Fatigue degrades your attention and your concentration. It also impairs coordination and makes you worse at communicating. Together these seriously weaken your ability to make good decisions.
It can be physical or mental. Sleep loss, exercise or physical work bring on the physical kind, while stress and long stretches of mental work bring on the other.
For your scan, attention matters most, especially your ability to divide it between several jobs at once. Flying asks for that split on every leg.

article.heading: Why your scan shrinks toward the middle
paragraphs: Skill fatigue, a type of acute or short-term fatigue, shows up in how you fly. Its first effect is on timing, with each step of a task slightly off while the whole looks normal. You end up flying the steps as separate pieces instead of one smooth action.

Its second effect narrows what you see. Your attention settles on movements and objects in the center of your vision, and the periphery, the outer part of your view, gets neglected. Your control inputs lose accuracy and smoothness along with it.

Exhaustion on a night flight pushes the same way. A worn-out pilot tends to work one aspect of a situation and miss the total of what it needs. Instead of a proper scan, you may fixate on the instruments or stare off, and stop handling several tasks.

Taken far enough, this becomes fixation, locking your attention on one goal or object while ignoring the cues that show your orientation. It tends to set in while you concentrate on the instruments or on a landing. You lock onto one task and forget to look at what is going on around you.
That is how traffic gets missed. Whether you spot an aircraft on a collision course depends partly on where you are looking.

article.heading: Why one task crowds out the rest
paragraphs: Fatigue, like stress or work overload, can lock you onto one item that seems important. Your awareness of the rest of the flight shrinks around it.

Distractions often start small. A gauge that is not reading right draws you in, and you stop monitoring the instruments and scanning outside. Control of the airplane is what slips while you work on it.

Workload makes it worse. As it climbs, you can no longer give attention to several tasks at one time, and you may begin to focus on one. At task saturation, having more to do than you can take in, input from other sources stops registering.

So fatigue removes the very skill a busy cockpit calls for, which is dividing your attention. Tasks also increase significantly in the landing phase, where the flying calls for more precision and attention.

figure.caption: When task requirements rise above what a pilot can handle, some tasks are done poorly and others are not done at all.
figure.alt: When task requirements rise above what a pilot can handle, some tasks are done poorly and others are not done at all.

article.heading: How a long night flight adds to it
paragraphs: Stack late nights and fatigue on sustained flight above 5,000 feet, and you may grow less discerning and less decisive. You may also question information less and become more compliant and accepting.
The timing makes it dangerous. Take a night instrument approach in the weather after a 4-hour flight, the most demanding stretch of the trip. It arrives when your guard is down the most.

By the end of a long flight day, fatigue and low-altitude hypoxia, too little oxygen for the body, have drained much of your energy. The handbook describes the result as a shift from deciding to accepting.

Your eyes take a hit as well. Above 4,000 feet pressure altitude, night vision drops measurably unless you are on supplemental oxygen, and fatigue makes the loss worse. At 12,000 feet at night, parts of your normal vision may be missing or out of focus.

article.heading: Why feeling fine tells you little
paragraphs: Ask a fatigued pilot who has flown 16 hours if they are too tired to keep flying. The answer may be no.
Flying alone, you act as your own quality control. The tired mind that is missing things is the same one judging whether it is missing them.
Most pilots are goal oriented. Offered a flight, they tend to deny their own limits and give weight to things that have no bearing on the trip.

That makes fatigue one of the hardest hazards to catch, since it may not be apparent until you have made serious errors. Fatigued pilots have fallen asleep while flying, yet the effects may be subtle, such as dulled thinking and weaker decisions.

article.heading: How IMSAFE asks the question for you
paragraphs: Since feel is unreliable, use a checklist that asks the question for you. IMSAFE is a self-check for before every flight, and it stands for Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue and Emotion.

The fatigue item asks whether you are tired and not adequately rested. Too little sleep is one cause, so start with how you slept rather than how you feel. Hypoxia and your emotional state can both intensify it.

Rest and 8 hours of sound sleep ordinarily cure acute fatigue. Sleep only corrects that kind, though. Chronic fatigue, which lasts over a long period, can involve several factors and needs more analysis and a remedy of its own.
The check does not stop at takeoff. On any flight longer than 2 hours, run the 5 P check, a review that includes you as the pilot, every hour.

posts.title: Stall speed rising with bank angle
posts.headline: Steepen a level turn and your stall speed rises.
posts.alt: Stall speed rising with bank angle: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A steeper level turn raises your stall speed. The picture shows a rendered single-engine aircraft heeled hard over in a steep turn, wings near sixty degrees of bank; the nose held on the horizon so the steep turn reads as level, not descending; a pale ghost of the same aircraft in a shallow bank, wings close to level; a thin level reference line joining solid aircraft and ghost at the same altitude. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Halfway around the steep turn the horn chirps, and the airspeed needle hasn't moved.

The wing is holding you up and hauling you around the corner at the same time. In a level turn, load factor grows with bank angle. Stall speed follows the square root of that load. Same airplane, higher number.

That number never shows up on the panel. The needle reads the same as it did wings level, so the margin feels unchanged. It has shrunk. The Airplane Flying Handbook works through steep turns in chapter 5.
FlightDecide computes the weight and balance for your planned load, so the gross weight behind your published stall speeds is a number you already have.
Next steep turns with your instructor, note the speed where the buffet starts and compare it to the wings level figure.
teaches: In a level turn load factor increases with bank angle.
Stall speed increases with the square root of the load factor, so a 60 degree level turn doubles the load and raises the stall speed by about 41 percent.
posts.intent: A level turn raises load factor and the stall speed rises with the square root of it, so a steep turn stalls at a higher speed.

article.heading: Why a steep turn stalls sooner
paragraphs: Picture yourself holding altitude at a steady airspeed and rolling into a 60 degree bank. The airspeed has not changed. Yet the airplane is now closer to a stall than it was a moment ago.

The reason is the extra work the wing is doing. In a level turn it has to hold up the airplane's weight and pull it around the corner at the same time. The steeper the bank, the harder the wing works.
That extra work has a name, load factor, and the stall speed rises with it. At 60 degrees of bank, the FAA's Airplane Flying Handbook puts the rise at 41 percent over the wings level stall speed.

article.heading: What load factor means
paragraphs: Load factor is the load the wing carries compared with the airplane's weight. Flying straight and level, the wing carries exactly the weight, and that is 1G. At 2G the wing is carrying twice the weight.
In a turn, the wing's lift tilts with the airplane. Part of it now points toward the center of the turn and pulls you around. Only the rest is left pointing up against the weight.

To stay level, you ask the wing for more lift in total. The more you bank, the more of that lift goes sideways, and the more total lift you need. So in a level turn, load factor grows with bank angle.

In a coordinated, level 60 degree bank, the load factor is 2G. Coordinated means the ball in the slip/skid indicator is centered. The wing is now holding up twice the airplane's weight at the same airspeed.

figure.caption: In the bank, the tilted lift has to grow to twice the weight so that its upward part still matches the weight.
figure.alt: In the bank, the tilted lift has to grow to twice the weight so that its upward part still matches the weight.

article.heading: How the square root sets the number
paragraphs: Stall speed does not rise at the same rate as load factor. It rises with the square root of the load factor. So when the load doubles, the stall speed goes up by 41 percent rather than doubling.
That softens the jump, but only a little. A 41 percent rise is a big change to a number that is easy to treat as fixed.

Take the wings level stall speed you learned for your own airplane. In a coordinated, level 60 degree bank, the stall comes at that figure plus 41 percent. The handbook gives no stall speed for any one airplane, so do the sum with yours.

table.caption: The same airplane at the same airspeed, wings level and in a level 60 degree turn.

article.heading: Why the stall follows angle of attack
paragraphs: To make that extra lift at the same airspeed, you raise the angle of attack. Angle of attack is the angle at which the wing's chord, a straight line from leading to trailing edge, meets the oncoming air.
As that angle grows, lift grows and so does drag. Each wing has a limit to that angle. Beyond it, the airflow separates from the top surface, lift drops and drag climbs. That is a stall.
The handbook is firm here. A stall comes from exceeding that limiting angle, not from a lack of airspeed. Stall speed is only the airspeed at which you reach the limit under one set of conditions.

In a 2G turn you are already holding a higher angle of attack than you did wings level. You sit closer to the limit, and so closer to the higher stall speed. That is why the handbook says you can stall at any airspeed, in any attitude and at any power setting.

Load factor is one of several things that set stall speed. Gross weight, center of gravity and flap setting move it too. Stall speed is not a constant, and the handbook wants you to understand what moves it.

article.heading: What changes when you are already slow
paragraphs: In slow flight practice you fly a target speed just above the stall warning. The handbook suggests 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed. That margin is measured against a wings level stall.
At that speed, any further increase in angle of attack or load factor, or any cut in power, brings a stall warning. Rolling into a steeper bank is exactly that kind of load factor increase.
Put the two numbers side by side. Your margin was 5 to 10 knots over the 1G stall speed. Steepen the bank and the stall speed itself climbs toward the speed you are flying.
Reduced airspeeds are normal on takeoff and departure, and on approach and landing. Those are also the phases flown close to the ground. A turn there adds load factor to a speed that was already low.

article.heading: What the airplane tells you first
paragraphs: A stall warning comes before the stall itself. It shows up as buffet, a shaking you feel through the airframe, or as the stall horn sounding.
The handbook says to react to and correct for any stall indication. A stall can lead to loss of control if the angle of attack is not reduced.

The stall speeds you learn for your airplane are 1G figures for one weight and configuration. In a steep level turn, the warning arrives at a speed that would give you room to spare wings level. Knowing why keeps it from being a surprise.
The aim, in slow flight and in turns, is to maneuver without setting off the stall warning at all. Knowing that 60 degrees of bank means 2G and a 41 percent higher stall speed is what lets you do it.

posts.title: Losing the headwind on final
posts.headline: A decreasing headwind costs airspeed and drops you below the path.
posts.alt: Losing the headwind on final: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A decreasing headwind costs airspeed and drops you below the path. The picture shows two wind layers divided by a soft shear seam: long streamlines above, short stubby ones below; a dashed intended glidepath running straight down to the runway threshold; the solid aircraft sitting beneath that dashed path, just after crossing the seam; a pale ghost of the same aircraft still on the dashed path at the same point along final. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Headwind loss on final arrives late in the approach, where you have the least altitude to spare.

On final you are low and committed to a path. The wing knows only the air moving over it right now. Pattern altitude is history. A headwind that weakens as you descend hands you a sink you never asked for.

It is easy to read the sag as your own flying. The air changed. The Airplane Flying Handbook covers this in its approach and landing chapter. The speed does come back. You are lower than you planned by the time it does.
FlightDecide reads the wind lines in your TAF for the planned window, including a low level wind shear group when the forecast carries one.
One sentence worth carrying down final: the speed sagged because the air changed, and the airplane is already going low.
teaches: A decreasing headwind with descent produces a momentary loss of indicated airspeed.
The aircraft sinks below the intended path, and getting the airspeed back does not by itself return it to the path.
The pilot must recover the path, promptly adding power and adjusting pitch to correct for the wind's effect on the descent.
posts.intent: Descending out of a stronger wind into a weaker one costs airspeed, and the aircraft sinks below the path while it recovers.

article.heading: What it looks like on final
paragraphs: You are established on final, trimmed and descending toward your aiming point. Then the airspeed sags without you touching the throttle or the yoke. A moment later the view through the windscreen says you are lower than you planned.
It is natural to blame your own flying and start chasing the needle. In this case the cause is the air. The headwind you had higher up has grown weaker as you came down.

That change is wind shear, a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a short distance, usually from one height to another. It can be reported, but it often goes undetected until you fly into it.
Moderate turbulence usually brings variations in indicated airspeed too. This is different. It is a loss tied to your descent through one layer of air into another.

article.heading: Why a weaker headwind costs airspeed
paragraphs: Your wing only responds to the air flowing over it. Indicated airspeed, the speed on your airspeed indicator, measures that flow. It says nothing about your speed over the ground.

In a strong headwind, the air is streaming toward you as you fly into it. Descend into a layer where that stream is slower, and the airplane at first carries its old motion. Less air now meets the wing, so indicated airspeed drops.
Nothing is wrong with the engine or the trim. The airplane has simply not caught up with the new air yet. That lag is why the loss is momentary.
The Aviation Weather Handbook notes that shear causes abrupt changes in an airplane's horizontal movement. On final, a weakening headwind is one of those changes, and you feel it as lost airspeed.

article.heading: Why getting the speed back is not enough
paragraphs: While the speed is low, the wing makes less lift than it did a moment before. The airplane sinks faster than your planned descent. The handbooks tie slow airspeed and too little lift directly to an airplane settling.
Your glidepath, the planned line from you down to the aiming point, stays where it was. The airplane has dropped under it. As the airplane settles into the new air, the airspeed returns.
Getting that speed back does not lift you back to the line. You come out of the sag at the right speed and the wrong height. The gap stays until you fix it.
This is why the timing matters. Low level shear is especially hazardous because the airplane is close to the ground. On final there is very little height left to lose.

figure.caption: The airspeed comes back without any help from you, but the height lost during the dip stays lost until you add power.
figure.alt: The airspeed comes back without any help from you, but the height lost during the dip stays lost until you add power.

article.heading: How to get back on the path
paragraphs: The recovery is about the height as much as the speed. Add power promptly, and adjust pitch to correct for what the wind did to your descent. Waiting for the speed to return by itself leaves you low.

Pitch alone will not do it. The Airplane Flying Handbook explains that when you are slow, raising the nose cuts airspeed further and greatly steepens the descent. Raise it too far and the airplane settles rapidly on too little lift.
The same handbook warns never to try to stretch a glide to reach a spot. Pulling back to hold the path without adding power is exactly that stretch.

It helps to know your margin. In its accuracy approaches, the handbook uses 1.3 VSO on final, where VSO is the stall speed with the airplane configured to land. A sag in airspeed comes straight out of that margin.
Correcting the wind's effect on your descent is the real goal. The airspeed is only the first thing the shear took from you.

article.heading: What makes the wind change near the ground
paragraphs: Wind that changes sharply at low height has many sources. The handbook lists terrain, temperature inversions, sea breezes, frontal systems and strong surface winds.

A temperature inversion is a layer where the air gets warmer with height instead of cooler. Inversions often sit in the lowest few thousand feet after the ground cools overnight. Strong wind shear often forms across them.

Thunderstorms add their own version. The gust front, the leading edge of wind flowing out from a storm, often runs as far as 15 mi ahead of the rain. It changes the surface wind rapidly and sometimes drastically.
A line of dust or debris along the ground, or spray across water, often marks where the gust front is at the surface.

article.heading: How big a change counts as shear
paragraphs: The handbook puts numbers on low level wind shear that does not come from storms. It is a change of 10 kt or more for every 100 ft of height.

That change has to happen in a layer more than 200 ft thick, within 2,000 ft of the surface. The handbook's practice patterns begin at approximately 1,000 feet above the ground, so your whole final sits inside that band.

This kind of shear is commonly tied to passing fronts, temperature inversions and strong upper-level winds, meaning greater than 25 kt. Some references also use the term severe wind shear, with thresholds of their own.

Severe wind shear can also mean shear that exceeds what the airplane is able to do. Wind shear can affect a flight at any altitude. Near the ground, it has long been counted a serious hazard on takeoff and approach.

posts.title: A temperature inversion trapping haze
posts.headline: The inversion that smooths the air also traps the haze below.
posts.alt: A temperature inversion trapping haze: an illustrated diagram for pilots. The inversion that smooths the air also traps the haze below. The picture shows a valley filled with dense haze whose top is cut off along one ruler-straight horizontal line; clean transparent air above that line with distant ranges still crisp and edged; a smoke column from a chimney that climbs vertically, stops dead at the line, and spreads sideways into a long level sheet; a small profile aircraft flying at the top of the haze with wings dead level. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Temperature inversions are stable layers, and stable air is what keeps the haze from clearing.

Vertical motion is what carries smoke and haze away. A stable layer has none, so it collects in the air you are looking through. Stability does all of it. The Aviation Weather Handbook covers inversions in chapter 18.

A smooth ride is easy to read as good conditions. It reports on mixing. With mixing suppressed, the haze underneath has nothing to lift it out and nowhere to go. Smooth air is what the trap feels like from inside.
FlightDecide reads the TAFs for your planned window and shows the forecast visibility and haze in a briefing you can check against raw data.
If the ride goes glassy and the horizon turns milky, one layer is doing both.
https://flightdecide.com iOS: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/flightdecide/id6761793626
teaches: A temperature inversion is a stable layer that suppresses vertical mixing.
The top of the inversion acts as a lid, trapping haze and smoke in the commonly smooth layer beneath it and reducing visibility there.
posts.intent: Smooth air and poor visibility arrive together, because the inversion that stops the mixing also traps what is in the air.

article.heading: The smooth ride with nothing to see
paragraphs: You climb out on a still morning and the air is glassy. There is no bump on the climb and the wings barely move. Yet the far end of the valley fades into a brown blur.

Those two things feel unrelated. One is good news for the ride and the other is bad news for finding your way. They come from the same layer of air, and once you see why, the pairing stops being a surprise.
That layer is called a temperature inversion. To understand it, start with what the air normally does as you climb.

article.heading: Why air usually gets colder with height
paragraphs: Air that rises moves into lower pressure, so it expands. Expanding air cools, even though no heat has left it. Air that sinks does the opposite, getting squeezed and warmer as the pressure grows.

This warming and cooling from pressure change alone is called adiabatic heating and cooling. The rate at which temperature drops with height is called the lapse rate. The handbook puts the average at 2 °C (3.5 °F) per 1,000 feet.
A parcel of air, a single blob you imagine lifting, cools at its own rate as it rises. Dry air cools faster than moist air. The rates sit side by side in the table below.

table.caption: How fast temperature falls with height, and the one layer where it does the reverse.

article.heading: What makes air keep rising or sink back
paragraphs: Picture nudging a parcel of air upward and then letting go. As it rises it cools, and you compare it with the air now around it. Colder air is denser, so a colder parcel sinks back to where it started.

If the parcel ends up warmer than its surroundings, it is lighter and keeps rising on its own. That is unstable air, where small upward pushes grow into bumps and building clouds. In stable air, small pushes die away instead.

The difference comes down to how fast the surrounding air cools with height. When it cools slowly, a lifted parcel soon ends up colder than its neighbours. The smaller the lapse rate, the more stable the air.

article.heading: Why rising air stalls at the warm layer
paragraphs: Now take the extreme case. In an inversion, the air gets warmer as you climb instead of colder, up to a certain height. That height is the top of the inversion.

Lift a parcel into that layer and it cools while the air around it warms. It ends up colder and denser than its surroundings, so it sinks back. The handbook files inversions under absolute stability, where every lifted parcel returns to its level.

This is why the ride is smooth. Vertical mixing, the up and down stirring of air that you feel as bumps, has nothing to drive it. The handbook describes these layers as commonly shallow, smooth and sitting close to the ground.

article.heading: Where the haze and smoke end up
paragraphs: Smoke, haze and other pollutants start near the surface. In unstable air, rising currents stir them upward through a deeper layer.
Under an inversion that stirring stops at the top of the layer. The warm air there works like a lid on a pot. Whatever is below stays trapped below it.
So the same stability that gives you a smooth ride also collects the haze. Visibility drops inside the layer, because what would have been carried upward is held in the shallow air near the ground.

Moisture adds to it. Relative humidity is how much water the air holds against the most it could hold at that temperature. When it is high, the trapped layer can also produce clouds, fog, haze or smoke.

article.heading: Where inversions come from
paragraphs: The most common kind starts at the ground. On a clear, cool night the ground loses heat and chills the air touching it. Soon the air within a few hundred feet of the surface is colder than the air above.

That is a surface-based inversion. The coldest air sits at the bottom, which is exactly the arrangement that resists mixing. That is why the smooth, hazy air in the opening section is a morning scene.
A second kind forms at fronts. Warm air spreads over a layer of cooler air, or cooler air pushes in underneath warmer air. Either way you get warm air on top of cold.

The sun changes the picture through the day. Daytime heating of the surface raises the lapse rate and lowers stability, while nighttime cooling does the opposite. The swing is largest over land, under clear skies, in dry air and light wind.

article.heading: What it means when you fly in it
paragraphs: Inside the layer, expect the ride to be smooth and the view to be poor. They are one state of the air showing up two ways. Treat a glassy ride as a prompt to look hard at visibility.
The top of the inversion is where things change. Climb above the lid and the haze lies below you as a level sheet. The reduced visibility the handbook describes belongs to the layer beneath.
Coming back down means descending into it again. Landmarks you picked out from above can fade once you sink under the lid, even though the air stays smooth the whole way.

posts.title: Lee-side downdraft
posts.headline: The air can sink faster than you can climb.
posts.alt: Lee-side downdraft: an illustrated diagram for pilots. The air can sink faster than you can climb.
caption: Lee-side downdraft: pitched up at climb power, an aircraft can still be losing height.

You plan a ridge crossing around climb performance. Descending air on the lee side can take that margin back, and FAA-H-8083-28 chapter 16 covers that flow. The margin goes first. The height goes next.
It is easy to read the attitude as proof of a climb. Pitch and power are inputs. The altimeter is the output. A steady nose-up picture can sit on top of a descending trend for the whole crossing.
FlightDecide computes the weight and balance for your planned flight window, which is one input to the climb performance you will have on the day.
If the nose is up and the altimeter is unwinding, believe the altimeter.
teaches: On the lee side of a ridge the air can be descending, and it can descend faster than a light aircraft climbs.
So a climb attitude does not guarantee a climb: the aircraft can be pitched up, at climb power, and still losing height.
When your route crosses mountain-wave flow, the handbook says to fly at turbulence penetration speed and avoid flying over terrain that drops abruptly.
Follow that advice even when there are no lenticular clouds, because the handbook warns the condition may have no cloud to mark it.
posts.intent: air spilling down the downwind side of a ridge can descend faster than a light aircraft can climb, even at a climb attitude

article.heading: Where the air goes after a ridge
paragraphs: Picture a steady wind blowing across a long ridge. The ridge forces that air up its windward face, the side the wind meets first. Once the air clears the crest, it heads back down the other side.
Why it comes back down is about stability. In stable air, air that has been lifted ends up heavier than the air around it. Gravity then pulls it back toward the level it came from.

It does not stop neatly at that level. Its momentum carries it too far, and on the way down it is warmed by compression until it is lighter than its surroundings. So it rises again, overshoots again, and keeps swinging up and down until the motion dies out.

That repeating up and down is a mountain wave, a wave in the air set up by the terrain. The handbook says a wave forms when the wind is strong enough and the air is stable. In unstable air with enough moisture, the same lift builds deep clouds or thunderstorms instead.

article.heading: Why the lee side sinks so hard
paragraphs: The downwind side of a ridge is called the lee side. When the wind blows roughly at right angles to the ridge, the air is pushed up and then sped up as it crosses the crest and runs down the lee slopes.

So on the lee side you are not in still air with a little sink in it. You are in air that is travelling downhill, and travelling fast. The handbook warns that these downdrafts can be faster than an aircraft can climb.

It singles out airplanes with high wing loading and high power loading. Wing loading is the weight each part of the wing has to carry. Power loading is the weight each unit of engine power has to lift.

How big the wave gets depends on the terrain and the wind. Its amplitude, how far the air is pushed up and down, is larger when the range stands higher above the land around it. A stronger wind across the ridge at mountaintop level also makes it larger.
Big mountains are not required. The handbook says even very modest terrain can produce appreciable wave activity when conditions are right.

article.heading: Why nose up does not mean going up
paragraphs: Your aircraft climbs relative to the air it is flying in. Pitch up, set climb power, and it rises through that body of air at its normal rate.
Now let that whole body of air sink faster than your climb rate. The two add together, and the result is a loss of height. You are climbing through the air while the air carries you down.
This is what makes the lee side confusing. The attitude indicator shows a climb attitude and the engine is at climb power. The altimeter keeps unwinding anyway.

The picture in the windscreen and the feel of the controls both say climb. Only the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator tell you the truth. On the lee side of a ridge, those are the instruments to believe.

article.heading: How strong the downdrafts get
paragraphs: The handbook gives figures for takeoff and landing near mountains in strong wind. Downdrafts greater than 1,500 fpm are possible. So are localized gusts in excess of 50 kt.

It also quotes a yardstick that some references use for severe wind shear. One version is wind shear that exceeds what the aircraft can do. Another is a vertical speed change greater than 500 fpm, or an airspeed change greater than 15 kt.
Put those side by side. A 1,500 fpm downdraft is three times the 500 fpm vertical change that already counts as severe by that yardstick.

Being low makes it worse. The handbook calls wind shear near the ground especially hazardous because the aircraft is so close to the terrain. It does not give a figure for sink rates at cruise height over a ridge, so none is offered here.

rows: Downdrafts near mountains, takeoff and landing
Localized gusts near mountains, takeoff and landing
Severe wind shear, vertical speed change

article.heading: What the handbook tells you to do
paragraphs: When your route crosses air flowing in a mountain wave, the handbook gives two pieces of advice. Fly at turbulence penetration speed. Stay away from flying over terrain that drops away abruptly.
Turbulence penetration speed is a speed chosen for flying through rough air. The handbook passage does not give a number for it.
The terrain advice follows from how the wave works. The air follows the lee slopes downhill and speeds up as it goes. Flying over a sharp drop puts you straight into that descending flow.
The handbook adds that wind shear, a sudden change in wind speed or direction, is greatly intensified in mountain wave conditions. That holds for shear in the vertical and in the horizontal.

article.heading: Why a clear sky proves nothing
paragraphs: The classic sign of a wave is lenticular cloud. These are smooth lens or airfoil shaped clouds that sit still downwind of a range, in bands parallel to it with clear gaps between. Rotor clouds and blowing dust are other signs.

Whether any cloud forms depends on the moisture in the air upwind. The handbook says these waves frequently occur with no cloud at all. It warns that extremely severe wind events can arrive with little or no visual warning.
So the advice holds with or without lenticulars. A blue sky over a ridge on a windy day is not evidence that the air behind it is calm.

The effects are not confined to low levels. Wave effects can reach far above the peaks, at times beyond 60,000 ft. The most severe mountain wind events usually come from late autumn to early spring, when the large-scale winds are strongest.

posts.title: Wind correction angle
posts.headline: Line up with where you are going, not where you are pointing.
posts.alt: Wind correction angle: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Line up with where you are going, not where you are pointing.
caption: Wind correction angle is what keeps your track on the extended centreline in a crosswind.

In a crosswind your heading and your track over the ground are two different things. The angle between them is the wind correction angle. On final, hold it into the wind. The track then stays down the extended centreline. The crab comes out before touchdown, so the aeroplane lands with its longitudinal axis on the runway.
It is easy to read a nose pointed straight at the runway as lined up. You drift when the correction is missing. Chapter 16 of FAA-H-8083-25 lays out the same wind triangle for cross country legs.
FlightDecide pulls wind direction and speed from the TAF for your planned window, then scores it in the go/no-go advisor.
On the next crosswind final, notice how far off the runway heading your nose sits while the track stays straight.
teaches: In a crosswind an aircraft's heading and its track over the ground are different, and the angle between them is the wind correction angle.
On the approach, holding a wind correction angle into the wind is what keeps the track along the extended centreline.
An aircraft that points straight at the runway in a crosswind, with no correction applied, drifts downwind of the centreline.
Taking the crab out the instant before touchdown aligns the axis with the runway, but aileron into the wind stops the drift.
posts.intent: in a crosswind the aeroplane's nose points off to one side while its path over the ground stays on the centreline

article.heading: Why your nose and your path disagree
paragraphs: Picture yourself flying at 90 knots with a 10 knot wind blowing from right to left. Through the air you still move forward at 90 knots. But the air is moving too, so it carries you 10 nautical miles to the left every hour.

Double your speed to 180 knots and that sideways drift does not shrink. You still move 10 nautical miles left each hour. Once you are airborne, you go wherever the air mass goes, whichever way the nose points.

That leaves you with two directions. Your heading is the way the nose points. Your track is the path you actually trace over the ground. In a crosswind they differ, and the angle between them is the wind correction angle.

article.heading: How far to turn into the wind
paragraphs: To fly a straight line over the ground, you angle the nose into the wind. Point far enough upwind and the sideways push is cancelled. Your track then runs straight to where you want to go.

Three things set the size of that angle. They are the wind speed, the angle between the wind and your longitudinal axis (the line from nose to tail), and your airspeed. More wind needs a bigger angle, and more airspeed needs a smaller one.
The handbook gives a worked pair. At 100 knots with 20 knots of wind straight from the side, you turn 12° into the wind. Halve the wind to 10 knots and the correction halves to six degrees.

A boat crossing a river works the same way. The captain angles the bow upstream so the boat's own motion matches the current pushing it downstream. A slower boat or a faster river needs a bigger angle.

table.caption: Wind correction angle for a wind directly from the side, from the handbook's example.

article.heading: What happens if you point at the runway
paragraphs: Now put yourself on final with the wind from the left. The runway sits dead ahead, so aiming the nose straight at it feels right. With no correction applied, the wind moves you sideways and you drift downwind of the centreline.

That drift builds up to the speed of the crosswind component, the part of the wind acting across your path. A wind directly from the side drifts you at its full speed. A wind at 45°, halfway between the nose and the side, drifts you at just over 70 percent of its speed.

So a nose aimed at the threshold tells you nothing about your track. Scan between references far ahead and close to the aeroplane. That is how you see whether you are holding the line or sliding off it.

article.heading: Holding the crab down final
paragraphs: The crab method, holding your heading off into the wind, puts the wind correction angle to work directly. You turn toward the wind until your wings-level ground track lines up with the runway centreline. The nose now sits off to the upwind side while you track straight down the extended centreline.
The wind rarely stays the same all the way down. Make small heading changes as needed to keep that alignment. You are flying the track, and the heading is whatever it takes to hold it.
The handbook calls the crab the easier method to keep up on final. The price comes at the bottom. Taking the crab out needs judgment and precise timing.

article.heading: Taking the crab out before touchdown
paragraphs: Tyres do not like landing sideways. When a loaded tyre's path and its heading differ, that difference is called the cornering angle, and it creates a side load. As little as 10° of cornering angle produces a side load equal to half the weight the tyre carries.

So you hold the crab until the instant before touchdown. Then you use rudder to swing the longitudinal axis into line with the direction you are moving. Straighten up too early or too late and the wheels meet the runway with a side load.

The round out, the flare just above the runway, is flown much like a normal one. You keep applying crosswind correction as needed to stop any drift. As you slow, the controls lose effect, so the correction you are holding becomes too small unless you add more.

article.heading: The wing-low method holds both together
paragraphs: The handbook recommends the wing-low method, also called a sideslip, in most cases. It keeps your track and your longitudinal axis on the centreline all the way to the ground. There is no heading change to time at the last moment.

First you use rudder to line the heading up with the runway. That leaves you in an uncorrected crosswind, so you start to drift. You then bank into the wind with aileron, just enough to cancel the drift.

More bank moves you upwind and less lets you slide downwind. Adjust both controls until you are tracking the centreline with the nose already straight. On a long final you can crab first and change smoothly to wing-low before the round out.
Keep the upwind wing down through the round out. Level the wings and the drift comes back, so you touch down moving sideways. Done well, the upwind main wheel touches first.

In a strong crosswind you lower the upwind wing further and need a lot of opposite rudder to stop the turn. If full opposite rudder still cannot hold the nose straight, the wind is too strong for that runway. Land on a better-aligned runway there or at an alternate.

figure.caption: Both methods keep you on the centreline, but the crab angles the nose into the wind while the wing-low method banks into it with the nose straight.
figure.alt: Both methods keep you on the centreline, but the crab angles the nose into the wind while the wing-low method banks into it with the nose straight.

posts.title: Density altitude
posts.headline: Thin air lengthens your takeoff and flattens your climb.
posts.alt: Density altitude: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Thin air lengthens your takeoff and flattens your climb.
caption: Density altitude takes thrust from the propeller and lift from the wing, and the runway does not grow.

Heat and elevation both thin the air. The field that felt long at seven in the morning is a different field at three in the afternoon. Your loading has not changed and neither has your technique. The ground roll grows anyway.

It is easy to treat runway length as the whole question. The climb gradient available is reduced on that same afternoon, and the rising ground past the departure end is still there. FAA-H-8083-25 chapter 11 has the performance side of this.
FlightDecide reads the TAF for your planned window and the weight and balance you entered, then scores both in one advisory.
After the longer ground roll, what is the other half of a density altitude problem?
teaches: Heat and elevation both thin the air, and thin air reduces the thrust the propeller makes and the lift the wing makes at a given speed.
Takeoff distance therefore grows with density altitude while the aircraft, its weight and the pilot's technique are all unchanged.
Rising terrain beyond the runway matters more on a thin-air day, because the climb gradient available is reduced at the same time as the ground roll is lengthened.
posts.intent: the same aeroplane uses far more runway to get airborne when the air is thin than when it is dense

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 11

article.heading: What thin air does to the same aeroplane
paragraphs: Picture one aeroplane at one weight, flown by one pilot, on two different days. On the first it lifts off with plenty of runway left. On the second it rolls and rolls before it will fly.
The difference is the air. Air density, the amount of air packed into a given space, sets how hard the air pushes back on the propeller and the wing.

Pilots put that density into a single number called density altitude. It is the height in the standard atmosphere, a reference model of pressure and temperature, where air is as dense as today's air. Your aeroplane performs as if it were at that height, whatever the field elevation says.
A high density altitude means thin air, and performance drops. A low density altitude means dense air, and performance improves.

article.heading: How height and heat each thin the air
paragraphs: The higher you go, the less air there is above you pressing down. With less pressure on it, air spreads out, so each cubic foot holds less of it.

The standard atmosphere puts sea level at 29.92 inHg, inches of mercury, and 15.0 °C. By 5,000 feet the standard pressure is down to 24.89 inHg. That is why Denver starts with thinner air than New Orleans before the weather has any say.
Heat thins the air as well. Warm air expands and takes up more room, so the same space holds less of it. From one airport to another across the country, temperature is the biggest driver of density.

Pressure altitude is what your altimeter reads when you set it to 29.92 inHg. The FAA weather handbook takes a pressure altitude of 10,000 ft with the air at 20 °C. The density altitude there is 12,700 ft.
Humidity adds a little on top. Water vapour is lighter than dry air, so moist air is less dense, though the handbooks treat the effect as small.

figure.caption: The same space holds less air when it is warmer or higher, which leaves the propeller and wing less to work with.
figure.alt: The same space holds less air when it is warmer or higher, which leaves the propeller and wing less to work with.

table.caption: Standard pressure and temperature both fall as you climb, from FAA-H-8083-25 Figure 11-2.

article.heading: Why the ground roll grows
paragraphs: Thin air hits the aeroplane in three ways at once. The engine takes in less air, so it makes less power. The propeller has less air to push back, so it makes less thrust.
The wing loses out too. Lift comes from air pressing on the wing, and lighter air presses less at the same speed.

Here is the part that catches pilots out. Your airspeed indicator shows nothing unusual, and you rotate at the usual indicated airspeed. Your true airspeed, your real speed through the air, is higher.

A higher true airspeed means a higher groundspeed at liftoff. So the aeroplane has to run faster along the runway before it will fly. It does that with less thrust to speed it up, which adds still more runway.
None of this needs a heavier load or a sloppier technique. The aeroplane and the pilot are exactly as they were. Only the air is different.

article.heading: How much longer, in the handbook's example
paragraphs: The Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25, works through one case. The altimeter, set to 29.92 inHg, shows a pressure altitude of 5,000 feet.

On a standard temperature day, the example has the POH, the pilot's operating handbook, calling for a ground run of 790 feet. On a standard day, pressure altitude and density altitude sit at the same level.
Now make the day 20 °C warmer than standard. The warm air expands, and the density altitude rises above 7,000 feet. The ground run in the example comes out closer to 1,000 feet.
Same runway, same aeroplane, same pilot. Those are the handbook's example figures, and your own aeroplane's numbers come from the manufacturer's performance charts.

table.caption: One pressure altitude, two temperatures, from the example in FAA-H-8083-25 chapter 11.
rows: 20 °C above standard, at 5,000 ft pressure altitude

article.heading: Why rising ground past the runway matters more
paragraphs: Getting off the ground is only half the job. Once airborne, you still have to climb away from whatever lies past the departure end.

Thin air cuts your rate of climb, because the engine and propeller have less to give. You also fly the climb at the usual indicated airspeed, which is a faster true airspeed. Covering more ground each minute while gaining less height gives a shallower climb angle.

On a hot day at a high field, both effects land together. You leave the ground later, further down the runway, then climb more gently from that later point. Hills you clear easily on a cold morning sit closer to your path.
So a runway that is long enough is not the same as a departure that works. The climb out over the ground beyond it needs checking against the same conditions.

article.heading: Working out density altitude before you go
paragraphs: You start with pressure altitude. Set 29.92 inHg on the altimeter and read it, or correct field elevation for the current altimeter setting.
The handbook's worked case is a sea level field with an altimeter setting of 29.7. Its table gives a correction of 205 feet, so the pressure altitude is 205 feet.
Next you correct that for temperature. A flight computer does it from pressure altitude and outside air temperature. The density altitude chart in chapter 11 does the same job on paper.
There is no rule of thumb or chart for humidity. On a warm, damp day, expect less performance than your dry-air numbers show.

posts.title: Which way the trim tab moves
posts.headline: Trim nose up and the tab goes down.
posts.alt: Which way the trim tab moves: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Trim nose up and the tab goes down.
teaches: On an elevator with a trim tab, such as a Cessna 172's, nose-up trim moves the tab down; the airflow under the tail pushes on the tab and holds the elevator's trailing edge up, relieving the back pressure the pilot was holding.

A stabilator, as on a Piper Cherokee, carries an antiservo tab that moves in the same direction as the stabilator's trailing edge, which firms up the control feel, and the same tab works as the trim device.
Set the attitude first and hold it with control pressure, then trim that pressure away; trim is not used to fly the airplane to an attitude.
In the Cessna 172S, forward rotation of the trim wheel trims nose down and aft rotation trims nose up.
posts.intent: Nose-up trim moves the elevator trim tab down, and the airflow on the tab holds the elevator up, so the back pressure the pilot was holding goes away.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 6

figure_key.label: TAB DOWN FOR NOSE UP
figure_key.points_at: The trim tab at the elevator's trailing edge, deflected down.

figure_key.label: AIRFLOW ON THE TAB
figure_key.points_at: The bunched streamlines pressing against the underside of the down-turned trim tab.

figure_key.label: ELEVATOR UP, NO BACK PRESSURE
figure_key.points_at: The elevator's raised trailing edge.

article.heading: Why you end up holding back pressure
paragraphs: Picture the start of a climb in a Cessna 172. You have chosen a pitch attitude, a place for the nose against the horizon. As the airspeed bleeds off, the nose wants to sink below it.
So you pull back on the control wheel, which pilots call back pressure. That raises the elevator, the hinged surface on the back of the horizontal tail.
Once the elevator is out of line with the airflow, the moving air pushes against it. That push is the force you feel through the wheel, and you have to keep resisting it.
Holding it ties up a hand and some of your attention for as long as the climb lasts. A trim system takes that steady pressure off you, so you can turn to other tasks.

The most common trim system on small airplanes is a single trim tab, a small hinged strip on the elevator's trailing edge. That is the back edge, the one the air leaves last. The 172S has one, worked by a trim wheel in the cockpit.

article.heading: Why the tab goes down for nose up
paragraphs: Roll in nose-up trim and the tab swings down, below the line of the elevator. Now it sticks out into the air flowing under the tail.
That air strikes the underside of the tab and pushes it up. The tab is hinged to the elevator, so the push lifts the elevator's trailing edge with it.

A raised elevator makes a downward force on the tail, so the tail moves down and the nose comes up. The air on the tab now holds the elevator up, which was your hand's job. That is why the back pressure goes away.
Nose-down trim is the mirror image. The tab goes up into the air flowing over the tail, which forces the elevator's trailing edge down. The tail rises and the nose lowers.

table.caption: The tab always goes one way and the elevator's trailing edge the other.

article.heading: Which way to turn the trim wheel
paragraphs: On an elevator with a trim tab, the tab and the elevator always move in opposite directions. You never need to picture the tab to trim correctly, though.
The 172S uses a vertically mounted trim wheel. Roll it aft and you trim nose up, and roll it forward to trim nose down.
That lines up with the control wheel, where aft raises the nose too. The trim control in the flight deck includes a trim tab position indicator, so you can see where the tab is set.
Let the pressure tell you what to do. If you are holding steady back pressure, you need nose-up trim. Keep rolling the wheel until that nose-heavy feel is gone.
In the climb from the top of this page, that means rolling the trim wheel aft. Nose-up trim lets you keep the climb attitude without holding back on the control wheel.

figure.caption: Roll the 172's trim wheel aft, the rim facing you moving down, and the pointer moves toward NOSE UP.
figure.alt: Roll the 172's trim wheel aft, the rim facing you moving down, and the pointer moves toward NOSE UP.

article.heading: Set the attitude first, then trim
paragraphs: Trim holds an attitude. It is not how you get to one. First set the power, the pitch attitude and the configuration, such as the flap setting, and hold the attitude with control pressure.
Then trim that pressure away until the airplane keeps the attitude with no force from you. Any force you feel after that should be one you chose, for a planned change of attitude.

The common mistake is the reverse, winding the trim wheel to move the nose. That is flying the airplane with the trim, and experienced pilots slip into it too. A related error is overcontrolling with trim, cranking in more than the airplane needs.

Each change of power, pitch attitude or configuration brings new control pressures. In most airplanes, the nose tends to drop as you reduce power, since less air from the propeller then flows over the tail. Set the new attitude, hold it, and retrim.
Steep turns are a good example. Once the bank goes beyond 30°, trimming away some of the extra back pressure may help. You may then need forward pressure on the rollout until you adjust the trim.

figure.caption: First hold the attitude you want with control pressure; then trim until that pressure is gone.
figure.alt: First hold the attitude you want with control pressure; then trim until that pressure is gone.

article.heading: Why a stabilator tab moves the same way
paragraphs: Everything so far is about an elevator with a trim tab, like the 172's. A Piper Cherokee has a stabilator instead, a one-piece horizontal tail that swings about a central pivot point.
Pull back and the stabilator's trailing edge rises, raising the nose. Because the entire surface moves, it is very sensitive to your inputs and to air loads.

To make it less touchy, it carries an antiservo tab, a tab that moves the same way as the stabilator's trailing edge. A linkage raises the tab when the trailing edge rises and lowers it when the trailing edge drops. That is the reverse of the 172's elevator tab.
Air on a tab that moves with the surface pushes the stabilator back into line with the airflow, against your hand. So it takes more force to move, and you are less likely to overcontrol it.

The same tab also works as the Cherokee's trim device. It relieves the control pressure and keeps the stabilator where you set it. You use it as you would an elevator tab, trimming away whatever pressure you are holding once the attitude is set.

figure.caption: On a stabilator, pulling back raises the trailing edge; the antiservo tab moves the same way, and the air on it pushes back, which is the firmer feel.
figure.alt: On a stabilator, pulling back raises the trailing edge; the antiservo tab moves the same way, and the air on it pushes back, which is the firmer feel.
